arXiv:2609.10450v1 [math.PR] 09 Sep 2026

Aldous’ spectral gap phenomena
in stochastic exchange models

Pietro Caputo, Matteo Quattropani, and Federico Sau Address: Pietro Caputo
Università degli Studi Roma Tre Email address: pietro.caputo@uniroma3.it Address: Matteo Quattropani
Università degli Studi Roma Tre Email address: matteo.quattropani@uniroma3.it Address: Federico Sau
Università degli Studi di Milano Email address: federico.sau@unimi.it
Abstract.

We consider a broad class of exchange dynamics with arbitrary weighted graph or hypergraph update structures, which includes the Kipnis–Marchioro–Presutti (KMP) model and the energies of Kac’s walk on the sphere. These are conservative continuous-spin systems whose reversible measures are Dirichlet distributions. We prove that their spectral gap is always attained by a polynomial of degree at most two in the energy variables. Equivalently, through an intertwining with the associated discrete particle systems, the dominant mode is always represented by either a one-particle or a two-particle observable. We interpret this as a manifestation of an Aldous-type spectral gap phenomenon. In particular, the resulting two-particle spectral gap identity settles a recent conjecture of Alon and Puder.

We also characterize sharply when one particle suffices and when a genuinely two-particle mode dominates. Under a common rescaling of the Dirichlet parameters, segment-like geometries are precisely those for which the gap is always of one-particle type, mean-field geometries are precisely those for which it is always of two-particle type, and all other geometries exhibit a nontrivial transition.

The proof relies on the analysis of the so-called hidden model, a dual representation of the original process. The mechanism underlying the degree-two reduction is remarkably robust and extends to a much broader class of stochastic exchange models and their associated particle systems, including the harmonic process, the immediate exchange model, averaging-type processes, and nonreversible variants.

Finally, we analyze boundary-driven versions of the KMP model, in which the bulk exchange dynamics interacts with reservoirs, generally resulting in nonreversible processes. In contrast to the conservative setting, we prove that the spectral gap of a boundary-driven model is always of one-particle type.

Keywords:
Kipnis–Marchioro–Presutti model; stochastic exchange models; spectral gap; Aldous-type spectral gap identities; Kac’s walk; particle systems on hypergraphs.

1. Introduction, models and main results

Stochastic exchange models are a broad family of Markov processes in which a continuous quantity, such as energy, wealth, or mass, is randomly redistributed among agents interacting through the edges of a graph or hypergraph. These models play a prominent role across a variety of fields, ranging from statistical physics to economics and the social sciences. Important examples include the Kipnis–Marchioro–Presutti (KMP) model [KMP82], Kac’s walk on the sphere [Kac56, DSC00, CCL03, CLL20], the averaging process [AL12], the harmonic process [FG22], and the immediate exchange model [HP14].

A fundamental feature of these dynamics is their intertwining relation with discrete particle systems, which allows one to describe the action of the generator on polynomial observables in terms of interacting random walks on the underlying (hyper)graph. In this work we prove that the spectral gap of these models is always attained by a polynomial observable of degree at most two in the energy variables. In terms of the associated particle systems, this means that the dominant relaxation mode is always described by either a one-particle or a two-particle observable, a property that we refer to as an Aldous-type phenomenon.

The name originates from a conjecture of David Aldous concerning a different dynamics, namely the interchange process on graphs, asserting that the spectral gap is always realized by a one-particle eigenfunction. This conjecture was later proved for arbitrary weighted graphs in [CLR10]. An analogous statement was then conjectured for interchange processes on arbitrary weighted hypergraphs; see, for instance, [BC24, Conjecture 1.7]. In that generality, the conjecture remains open; see [AKP25, BC24] for some partial progress. See also [Ces16, AP26, LP26] and references therein for some further related results.

In the setting of stochastic exchange models, however, it is known that one-particle eigenfunctions do not suffice in general, and that genuinely two-particle observables are sometimes required; see, e.g., [CLL20, Remark 4]. It remained, however, to understand whether two particles are always sufficient to characterize the spectral gap. Related phenomena and questions have recently been investigated for a broad class of stochastic exchange models in [KQS25], for the symmetric inclusion process and the related diffusion [KS24, KS26], and for random walks on the unitary group generated by weighted hypergraphs in [AP26]. These works provide substantial progress and proved the validity of Aldous-type phenomena in several special cases, but the question of whether two particles always suffice remains unresolved.

The present work settles this issue in the affirmative for stochastic exchange models, answering several questions raised in [KQS25]. It also proves a conjecture of Alon and Puder stated in [AP26, Conjecture 1.15], yet, not addressing the more general statement concerning random walks on the unitary group formulated in [AP26, Conjecture 1.14].

1.1. KMP models: Aldous’ spectral gap phenomenon

Let n≥2n\geq 2, [n]≔{1,…,n}[n]\coloneqq\{1,\ldots,n\}, and consider the simplex

(1.1) Ω≔{η∈[0,1]n:∑x∈[n]ηx=1}​.\textstyle\Omega\coloneqq\big\{\eta\in[0,1]^{n}:\sum_{x\in[n]}\eta_{x}=1\big\}\,\text{.}

In the original KMP model, (ηx)x∈[n](\eta_{x})_{x\in[n]} represent the energies in a one-dimensional chain of oscillators, and at rate one independently each pair (ηx,ηx+1)(\eta_{x},\eta_{x+1}), x=1,…,n−1x=1,\dots,n-1, undergoes exchange updates

(1.2) (ηx,ηx+1)⟼(U⁡(ηx+ηx+1),(1−U)​(ηx+ηx+1))​,(\eta_{x},\eta_{x+1})\longmapsto(U(\eta_{x}+\eta_{x+1}),(1-U)(\eta_{x}+\eta_{x+1}))\;\text{,}\;\;

where UU is a uniform random variable in [0,1][0,1]. In the absence of external reservoirs, the total energy ∑x=1nηx=1\sum_{x=1}^{n}\eta_{x}=1 is conserved—hence, we sometimes speak of the conservative KMP{\rm KMP} model—and the equilibrium measure is simply the uniform distribution over Ω\Omega. Convergence to stationarity for this model was extensively analyzed in [CLL20], which, among other things, proved that the spectral gap is given by λ=1−cos⁡(π/n)\lambda=1-\cos(\pi/n) with the linear eigenfunction

(1.3) η⟼∑y=1n−1sin⁡(π​y/n)​∑x=1y(ηx−1n).\eta\longmapsto\sum_{y=1}^{n-1}\sin(\pi y/n)\sum_{x=1}^{y}\left(\eta_{x}-\tfrac{1}{n}\right)\,.

If one replaces the graph segment {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} by the complete graph over nn vertices, computations as in [CCL03, Cap08] show that the spectral gap is now given by λ=(n+1)/3\lambda=(n+1)/3 with the quadratic eigenfunction

(1.4) η⟼∑x=1n(ηx2−2n⁡(n+1))​.\eta\longmapsto\sum_{x=1}^{n}\left(\eta_{x}^{2}-\tfrac{2}{n(n+1)}\right)\,\text{.}

In this work, we consider a generalized version of the KMP model where the underlying graph is a completely arbitrary weighted hypergraph, and the redistribution variable UU in (1.2) is replaced by a general inhomogeneous Dirichlet distribution. While there are no closed formulas for the spectral gap and the associated eigenfunction in this generality, we shall prove that, for the conservative KMP model, the dominant mode is always a polynomial of degree at most two. In contrast, we show that polynomials of degree one always suffice for its non-conservative variant; see Section 1.3.2.

(1.5) ηB⟼η⁡(B)​U​,U=(Ux)x∈B∼Dir⁡(αB)​,​η​(B)≔∑x∈Bηx​.\textstyle\eta^{B}\longmapsto\eta(B)U\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad U=(U_{x})_{x\in B}\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha^{B})\;\text{,}\;\;\eta(B)\coloneqq\sum_{x\in B}\eta_{x}\,\text{.}

Note that when B={x,x+1}B=\{x,x+1\} and αx=αx+1=1\alpha_{x}=\alpha_{x+1}=1, (1.5) coincides with the exchange update in (1.2). 1.1.2. Particle systems and second main result

As a starting point, we observe that the invariance property (1.10) admits a sharper formulation: the action of ℒ\mathcal{L} on polynomials transfers to a particle system’s generator acting on their coefficients. We now recall some basic facts, postponing all the details to Section 2.1.

Fix k≥1k\geq 1. Since ∑x∈[n]ηx=1\sum_{x\in[n]}\eta_{x}=1 on Ω\Omega, every element of 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} can be represented in homogeneous degree kk form. Thus, any polynomial in 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} takes the form

(1.14) ℒ​ψ^=Lk​ψ^​,\mathcal{L}\widehat{\psi}=\widehat{L_{k}\psi}\;\text{,}\;\;

where LkL_{k} denotes the generator of a labeled kk-particle system on [n]k[n]^{k}. The dynamics is as follows. Start with kk labeled particles at positions x1,…,xk∈[n]x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in[n]. Whenever a block BB is selected, at rate wBw_{B}, sample U∼Dir⁡(αB)U\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha^{B}). Each particle currently sitting in BB is then resampled inside BB, conditionally independently given UU, according to

(1.15) xi∈B⟼y∈Bwith probability ​Uy​,x_{i}\in B\longmapsto y\in B\quad\text{with probability }U_{y}\;\text{,}\;\;

whereas particles outside BB are kept fixed. After averaging over the block updates and over the Dirichlet vectors, one obtains the Markov generator LkL_{k}; see (2.4) below for the explicit expression. We call the resulting process on [n]k[n]^{k} the KMP{\rm KMP} labeled-particle system or, more precisely, the discrete (k,α,w)(k,\alpha,w)-KMP model.

When k=1k=1, the dynamics reduces to a random walk. Indeed, writing

(1.16) α⁡(B)≔∑z∈Bαz​,​B⊆[n]​,rx​y​(α,w)=αy​∑B∋x,ywBα⁡(B)​,​x≠y​,\alpha(B)\coloneqq\sum_{z\in B}\alpha_{z}\;\text{,}\;\;B\subseteq[n]\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad r_{xy}(\alpha,w)=\alpha_{y}\sum_{B\ni x,y}\frac{w_{B}}{\alpha(B)}\;\text{,}\;\;x\neq y\;\text{,}\;\;

For k≥2k\geq 2, the particles genuinely interact: several may jump during the same block update, and their transition probabilities are sampled from the same random vector UU.

Just as ℒ\mathcal{L} in (1.6) is a block heat-bath generator with respect to μ=Dir⁡(α)\mu={\rm Dir}(\alpha), the kk-particle generator LkL_{k} admits an analogous interpretation. To identify the corresponding reference measure, let η∼μ\eta\sim\mu and, conditionally on η\eta, let X1,…,XkX_{1},\ldots,X_{k} be independent with common law η\eta on [n][n]. Namely, conditionally on the particles outside a block BB, the conditional resampling in (1.5) of ηB\eta^{B} under μ\mu and the identity μk(x1,…,xk)=μ(ηx1⋯ηxk)\mu_{k}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})=\mu(\eta_{x_{1}}\cdots\eta_{x_{k}}) imply that the particles lying in BB are redistributed independently according to a common random probability vector U∼Dir⁡(αB)U\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha^{B}). This is exactly the BB-update defining LkL_{k}. Hence, μk\mu_{k} is reversible for LkL_{k}, and LkL_{k} is self-adjoint on L2​(μk)=L2​([n]k,μk)L^{2}(\mu_{k})=L^{2}([n]^{k},\mu_{k}). Consequently, LkL_{k} has all real eigenvalues. In analogy with (1.11), we define gap⁡(Lk){\rm gap}(L_{k}) as the second smallest eigenvalue of −Lk-L_{k}.

As the representation in (1.13) depends only on the symmetric part of ψ:[n]k→ℝ\psi:[n]^{k}\to\mathbb{R}, the intertwining relation in (1.14) is fully informative only for symmetric functions ψ\psi in

(1.19) ℋk≔{ψ:ψ(xς⁡(1),…,xς⁡(k))=ψ(x1,…,xk)for allς∈𝔖k,x1,…,xk∈[n]},\mathscr{H}_{k}\coloneqq\big\{\psi:\psi(x_{\varsigma(1)},\ldots,x_{\varsigma(k)})=\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\ \text{for all}\ \varsigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{k},x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in[n]\big\}\;\text{,}\;\;

where 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} denotes the symmetric group on [k][k]. Since LkL_{k} clearly commutes with permutations of the labels, this subspace is LkL_{k}-invariant, and

corresponds to the generator of the unlabeled version of the same particle system. Equivalently, LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} describes the LkL_{k}-dynamics in which labels are forgotten and only the particle-occupation numbers at each site are retained.

As we shall prove in Proposition 2.3, the intertwining (1.14) shows that ℒ|𝒫k\mathcal{L}|_{\mathscr{P}_{k}} and LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} are isospectral, see (2.27); thus,

(1.22) gap⁡(Lksym)=gap⁡(ℒ|𝒫k)=gap⁡(ℒ|𝒫2)=gap⁡(L2sym)​,k≥2​.{\rm gap}(L_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}})={\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}|_{\mathscr{P}_{k}})={\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}|_{\mathscr{P}_{2}})={\rm gap}(L_{2}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 2\,\text{.}

In other words, for arbitrary positive site weights α\alpha and nonnegative block weights ww, the unlabeled particle systems satisfy a two-particle spectral gap identity. In the special case α≡1\alpha\equiv 1, this is precisely the particle-system identity predicted by [AP26, Conjecture 1.15]; hence, Theorem 1.1 settles that conjecture.

We now turn to the labeled dynamics. The operator LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} is obtained by restricting LkL_{k} to the subspace of symmetric observables; this restriction is proper exactly when k≥2k\geq 2. Consequently, the spectrum of LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} is contained in that of LkL_{k}, and, in particular,

(1.23) gap⁡(Lk)≤gap⁡(Lksym)​,k≥1​.{\rm gap}(L_{k})\leq{\rm gap}(L_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 1\,\text{.}

Our second main result shows that this inequality always saturates to an identity.

Theorem 1.2 (Discrete KMP).

For all positive site weights α\alpha and all nonnegative block weights ww, the spectral gap of the discrete (k,α,w)(k,\alpha,w)-KMP{\rm KMP} model satisfies

(1.24) gap⁡(Lk)=gap⁡(Lksym)​,k≥1​.{\rm gap}(L_{k})={\rm gap}(L_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 1\,\text{.}

Together with (1.22), this yields

(1.25) gap⁡(Lk)=gap⁡(L2sym)​,k≥2​.{\rm gap}(L_{k})={\rm gap}(L_{2}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 2\,\text{.}
Remark 1.3.

The identity in (1.25) in Theorem 1.2 is a strengthening of Theorem 1.1: the identity in (1.22) identifies the gap over symmetric observables as being governed by the two-particle system, while (1.25) further proves that non-symmetric observables contribute no smaller eigenvalues.

The spectral gap identity in (1.25) shows that at most two particles always suffice to determine the KMP{\rm KMP} spectral gap. As we shall see, both this phenomenon and the mechanism behind its proof are remarkably robust, extending to a broad class of stochastic exchange models and their associated particle systems; see Sections 1.3.3 and 7.

For KMP{\rm KMP} models, however, these ideas can be sharpened considerably: according to the weights α\alpha and the geometry encoded by ww, they determine whether the gap is already attained by a degree-one polynomial or instead requires a genuinely degree-two polynomial, thereby revealing a sharp dichotomy between one-particle and two-particle domination. We develop this characterization in the next subsection.

Remarkably, the segment and the complete graph—and their weighted-hypergraph analogues—emerge as the only two distinct geometries for which one of these quantities uniformly dominates the other.

1.2.3. Characterization of the extremal geometries

The case τc​(α,w)=0\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0 is the regime in which the KMP spectral gap is always determined by gap1​(τ​α,w){\rm gap}_{1}(\tau\alpha,w), whereas τc​(α,w)=∞\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=\infty corresponds to the opposite regime, in which it is always determined by gap2,∗​(τ​α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\tau\alpha,w). We shall show that these two extremal cases correspond, respectively, to segment-like and mean-field geometries, while all remaining weighted hypergraphs exhibit a genuine phase transition, with τc​(α,w)∈(0,∞)\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)\in(0,\infty). This classification applies to general weighted hypergraphs and goes substantially beyond the previously known cases mentioned above, as well as the extension conjectured in [CLL20, Remark 3].

For clarity, we first state the characterization for weighted graphs (Theorem 1.6), where the relevant geometries take a particularly transparent form, and then turn to the general hypergraph setting (Theorem 1.8).

Graph case.

Here, we focus on graphs, namely, on weights ww supported on size-two blocks:

Since the segment condition (1.42) depends only on the graph weights ww, whereas the mean-field condition (1.43) imposes a specific relation between α\alpha and ww, fixing ww as in Theorem 1.6 yields the following dichotomy:

    Either ww induces a segment as in (1.42), and

Hypergraph case.

For general hypergraphs satisfying only (1.35)–(1.36), an analogous picture remains valid after passing to a suitable partition, as we explain below; then, the extremal regimes τc​(α,w)∈{0,∞}\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)\in\{0,\infty\} are characterized, respectively, by hypergraph analogues of the segment and mean-field graphs.

Given block weights w=(wB)B⊆[n]w=(w_{B})_{B\subseteq[n]}, we say that a partition

(1.46) [n]=N1⊔⋯⊔Nm​,2≤m≤n​,[n]=N_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup N_{m}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad 2\leq m\leq n\;\text{,}\;\;

If ww induces a connected graph (1.41), the discrete partition is in fact the only ww-compatible one. As already mentioned, for graph weights ww (i.e., satisfying (1.41)) on n≥3n\geq 3 sites, connectedness (1.36) forces the discrete partition [n]={1}⊔⋯⊔{n}[n]=\{1\}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\{n\} to be the coarsest one. Hence, Theorem 1.6 indeed follows from Theorem 1.8.

1.3. Related models and extensions

We next place the main spectral gap identity for the KMP model, established in Theorem 1.1, in a broader context. We first discuss analogous Aldous-type spectral gap phenomena for Kac’s walk on the sphere and heat-bath dynamics for cone measures, systems whose structure is richer than that of the KMP{\rm KMP} model. We then establish a degree-one spectral gap identity for the non-conservative KMP{\rm KMP} model and, finally, show that our main theorem extends to a broad class of stochastic exchange models.

1.3.1. Kac’s walk and generalizations

Kac’s walk on the sphere is the continuous-time Markov process on

(1.51) 𝕊≔{v∈ℝn:∑x∈[n]vi2=1}⊆ℝn​,\mathbb{S}\coloneqq\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\textstyle\sum_{x\in[n]}v_{i}^{2}=1\right\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\;\text{,}\;\;

defined as follows. Each unordered pair of coordinates {x,y}\{x,y\} is updated independently at rate 11. When an update occurs at the pair {x,y}\{x,y\}, the vector (vx,vy)(v_{x},v_{y}) is replaced by a new pair (vx′,vy′)(v_{x}^{\prime},v^{\prime}_{y}), chosen uniformly on the circle

(1.52) {(vx′,vy′)∈ℝ2:(vx′)2+(vy′)2=vx2+vy2}​.\{(v_{x}^{\prime},v_{y}^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:(v_{x}^{\prime})^{2}+(v_{y}^{\prime})^{2}=v_{x}^{2}+v_{y}^{2}\}\,\text{.}

The process is reversible with respect to the uniform distribution on 𝕊\mathbb{S}. Introduced by Kac in [Kac56] as a mean-field toy model for energy-preserving collisions in kinetic theory, this process has since been studied extensively. It was shown in [CCL03] that the spectral gap equals λ=(n+2)/4\lambda=(n+2)/4 with eigenfunction

(1.53) v⟼∑i=1n(vi4−3n⁡(n+2)),v\longmapsto\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(v_{i}^{4}-\tfrac{3}{n(n+2)}\right)\,,

a polynomial of degree 4 in the velocity variables v=(vx)x∈[n]v=(v_{x})_{x\in[n]}. We also refer to [Cap08] for an alternative computation of the spectral gap, and to [Mas03] for a characterization of all eigenvalues of this process.

In this work, we consider a generalization of Kac’s walk in two directions. First, the complete-graph geometry is replaced by a weighted hypergraph, allowing updates on arbitrary blocks and with arbitrary rate. Second, the Euclidean sphere 𝕊⊆ℝn\mathbb{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is replaced by the inhomogeneous ℓpn\ell_{p}^{n}-type sphere

(1.54) 𝕊p≔{ζ∈ℝn:∑x∈[n]|ζx|px=1}⊆ℝn​,\mathbb{S}_{p}\coloneqq\left\{\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\textstyle\sum_{x\in[n]}|\zeta_{x}|^{p_{x}}=1\right\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\;\text{,}\;\;

where p=(px)x∈[n]p=(p_{x})_{x\in[n]} is an arbitrary vector with positive entries.

We equip 𝕊p\mathbb{S}_{p} with the probability distribution κ\kappa given as follows. Let Z=(Zx)x∈[n]Z=(Z_{x})_{x\in[n]} be independent real random variables with densities proportional to z↦exp⁡(−|z|px)z\mapsto\exp(-|z|^{p_{x}}), and define

(1.55) Φp​(Z)≔∑y∈[n]|Zy|py​,ζx≔ZxΦp​(Z)1/px​,​x∈[n]​.\Phi_{p}(Z)\coloneqq\sum_{y\in[n]}|Z_{y}|^{p_{y}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\zeta_{x}\coloneqq\frac{Z_{x}}{\Phi_{p}(Z)^{1/p_{x}}}\;\text{,}\;\;x\in[n]\,\text{.}

Therefore, ζ∈𝕊p\zeta\in\mathbb{S}_{p} by construction, and its law κ\kappa is referred to as the cone measure on 𝕊p\mathbb{S}_{p}; see, e.g., [CS26] or [BGMN05] for a discussion of the homogeneous cases p≡const.>0p\equiv{\rm const.}>0. We note that when p≡2p\equiv 2 one recovers the uniform distribution over 𝕊\mathbb{S}.

For nonnegative block weights w=(wB)B⊆[n]w=(w_{B})_{B\subseteq[n]}, define the (p,w)(p,w)-Gibbs sampler, or heat-bath dynamics, for the cone measure, as the Markov process on 𝕊p\mathbb{S}_{p} with infinitesimal generator

(1.56) 𝒢​h​(ζ)≔∑B⊆[n]wB​(κB​h​(ζ)−h⁡(ζ))​,κB​h​(ζ)≔κ⁡(h∣ζBc)​.\mathcal{G}h(\zeta)\coloneqq\sum_{B\subseteq[n]}w_{B}\left(\kappa_{B}h(\zeta)-h(\zeta)\right)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\kappa_{B}h(\zeta)\coloneqq\kappa(h\mid\zeta^{B^{c}})\,\text{.}

with ζ∈𝕊p\zeta\in\mathbb{S}_{p} and h:𝕊p→ℝh:\mathbb{S}_{p}\to\mathbb{R} bounded and measurable. That is, with rate wBw_{B}, the block variables ζB=(ζx)x∈B\zeta^{B}=(\zeta_{x})_{x\in B} are resampled according to the conditional distribution κ\kappa given the variables ζBc=(ζx)x∉B\zeta^{B^{c}}=(\zeta_{x})_{x\notin B}. The generator 𝒢\mathcal{G} is, thus, a bounded self-adjoint operator in L2​(κ)=L2​(𝕊p,κ)L^{2}(\kappa)=L^{2}(\mathbb{S}_{p},\kappa). Observe that the case p≡2p\equiv 2 and wB=𝟙|B|=2w_{B}=\mathds{1}_{|B|=2} corresponds to Kac’s walk on the sphere.

For general p=(px)x∈[n]p=(p_{x})_{x\in[n]} and w=(wB)B⊆[n]w=(w_{B})_{B\subseteq[n]}, this dynamics admits a natural projection, under which it reduces to a KMP dynamics. More precisely, define, for all x∈[n]x\in[n],

(1.57) ηx≔|ζx|px​,σx≔sign⁡(ζx)​.\eta_{x}\coloneqq|\zeta_{x}|^{p_{x}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\sigma_{x}\coloneqq{\rm sign}(\zeta_{x})\,\text{.}

In this context, we refer to η=(ηx)x∈[n]\eta=(\eta_{x})_{x\in[n]} and σ=(σx)x∈[n]\sigma=(\sigma_{x})_{x\in[n]} as the energy and spin/angle variables of ζ\zeta, respectively. On the one hand, when ζ∼κ\zeta\sim\kappa, the corresponding energy variables η\eta belong to Ω\Omega and satisfy

(1.58) η=(ηx)x∈[n]∼Dir⁡(α)​,σ=(σx)x∈[n]​i.i.d. uniform on ​{±1}​,η⟂⟂σ,\eta=(\eta_{x})_{x\in[n]}\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\sigma=(\sigma_{x})_{x\in[n]}\ \text{i.i.d.\ uniform on }\{\pm 1\}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\eta\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma\,,

where αx=1/px\alpha_{x}=1/p_{x}, x∈[n]x\in[n], and where η⟂⟂σ\eta\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma indicates that η\eta and σ\sigma are independent. Indeed, the random variables |Zx|px|Z_{x}|^{p_{x}} are independent Gamma⁡(αx,1){\rm Gamma}(\alpha_{x},1); thus, their normalization by Φp​(Z)\Phi_{p}(Z) gives the law Dir⁡(α){\rm Dir}(\alpha). On the other hand, under the map ζ↦η\zeta\mapsto\eta, the (p,w)(p,w)-Gibbs sampler in (1.56) projects exactly onto the KMP{\rm KMP} model in (1.5) with parameters (α,w)(\alpha,w). Consequently, for this choice of parameters, spec⁡(ℒ)⊆spec⁡(𝒢){\rm spec}(\mathcal{L})\subseteq{\rm spec}(\mathcal{G}). Thus, the spectral gap of the Gibbs sampler, referred to as gap⁡(𝒢){\rm gap}(\mathcal{G}), is at most the spectral gap of ℒ\mathcal{L}, namely gap⁡(ℒ)=gap⁡(ℒ|𝒫2){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L})={\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}|_{\mathscr{P}_{2}}) as in Theorem 1.1. We shall establish that they coincide.

Theorem 1.10 (Gibbs sampler for cone measure).

For all positive site weights pp and all nonnegative block weights ww, the spectral gap of the (p,w)(p,w)-Gibbs sampler on 𝕊p\mathbb{S}_{p} satisfies

(1.59) gap⁡(𝒢)=gap⁡(ℒ|𝒫2)​,{\rm gap}(\mathcal{G})={\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}|_{\mathscr{P}_{2}})\;\text{,}\;\;

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is the generator of the (α,w)(\alpha,w)-KMP{\rm KMP} model with αx=1/px\alpha_{x}=1/p_{x}, x∈[n]x\in[n]. Moreover, it is attained by a polynomial eigenfunction of degree at most 22 in the energy variables ηx=|ζx|px\eta_{x}=|\zeta_{x}|^{p_{x}}.

Combined with Theorem 1.61 and Remark 1.7, this shows also that, in the graph case (1.41), the spectral gap of the (p,w)(p,w)-Gibbs sampler on 𝕊p\mathbb{S}_{p} is attained by a linear function in the energy variables ηx=|ζx|px\eta_{x}=|\zeta_{x}|^{p_{x}} for every choice of positive weights pp if and only if ww is a weighted segment. To the best of our knowledge, this and analogous claims which may be deduced by combining Theorems 1.4, 1.6, 1.8 and 1.10 are new even in the special case of Kac’s walk corresponding to p≡2p\equiv 2, for which previously only the homogeneous complete graph case (1.53) was understood.

1.3.2. Boundary-driven KMP{\rm KMP}

Consider the KMP{\rm KMP} model in which, in addition to the conservative exchange dynamics (1.5)–(1.6), the system exchanges energy with external reservoirs. Fix parameters ωx≥0\omega_{x}\geq 0 and βx,ρx>0\beta_{x},\rho_{x}>0, for x∈[n]x\in[n]. At rate ωx\omega_{x}, the energy at xx is updated according to

(1.60) ηx⟼Ux​(ηx+ξx)​,\eta_{x}\longmapsto U_{x}\left(\eta_{x}+\xi_{x}\right)\;\text{,}\;\;

while all other coordinates remain unchanged; at each such update, the pair (Ux,ξx)(U_{x},\xi_{x}) is sampled independently of the current configuration and of all previous updates, with

(1.61) (Ux,ξx)∼Beta⁡(αx,βx)⊗Gamma⁡(βx,ρx)​.(U_{x},\xi_{x})\sim{\rm Beta}(\alpha_{x},\beta_{x})\otimes{\rm Gamma}(\beta_{x},\rho_{x})\,\text{.}

Here, Gamma⁡(β,ρ){\rm Gamma}(\beta,\rho) denotes the gamma distribution whose density is proportional to s↦sβ−1e−s/ρs\mapsto s^{\beta-1}e^{-s/\rho} on [0,∞)[0,\infty). We write 𝐄x\mathbf{E}_{x} for expectation with respect to the product law in (1.61).

Letting ηx,Ux,ξx\eta^{x,U_{x},\xi_{x}} denote the configuration obtained from η\eta through (1.60), the reservoir generator is

(1.62) ℒ∂f(η)=∑x∈[n]ωx(𝐄x[f(ηx,Ux,ξx)]−f(η)),η∈Ωbd≔[0,∞)n,\mathcal{L}_{\partial}f(\eta)=\sum_{x\in[n]}\omega_{x}\,(\mathbf{E}_{x}\big[f(\eta^{x,U_{x},\xi_{x}})\big]-f(\eta))\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\eta\in\Omega_{\rm bd}\coloneqq[0,\infty)^{n}\;\text{,}\;\;

where ff is a bounded measurable function on Ωbd\Omega_{\rm bd}. The boundary-driven KMP generator is

(1.63) ℒbd=ℒ+ℒ∂​.\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}=\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{L}_{\partial}\,\text{.}

Here, ℒ\mathcal{L} denotes the conservative KMP{\rm KMP} generator associated with some block weights w=(wB)B⊆[n]w=(w_{B})_{B\subseteq[n]} and site weights α=(αx)x∈[n]\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in[n]}, introduced on Ω\Omega in (1.6) and naturally extended to Ωbd\Omega_{\rm bd} through the same update rules.

Assume that the hypergraph induced by ww is connected and that ω≢0\omega\not\equiv 0. In this general setting, it is possible to show that the boundary-driven process admits a unique invariant measure. However, we omit a detailed proof of this fact, as it will not be used in the proof of Theorem 1.11 below. In the special case in which ρx≡ρ∗\rho_{x}\equiv\rho_{\ast} is constant on supp⁡(ω){\rm supp}(\omega), one can check that the process admits an explicit, product, reversible measure, given by

(1.64) ν=⨂x∈[n]​Gamma​(αx,ρ∗)​.\nu=\underset{x\in[n]}{\bigotimes}{\rm Gamma}(\alpha_{x},\rho_{\ast})\,\text{.}

Thus, whenever ρx≡ρ∗\rho_{x}\equiv\rho_{\ast}, ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} is self-adjoint on L2​(ν)=L2​(Ωbd,ν)L^{2}(\nu)=L^{2}(\Omega_{\rm bd},\nu). If instead ρ\rho is non-constant on supp⁡(ω){\rm supp}(\omega), the process is non-reversible, and its invariant measure—usually referred to as its nonequilibrium steady state—is generally neither in product form nor explicit. Several important questions concerning this measure remain open, even on the segment. For further details, we refer to [DMFG24, GRT25], where the choice βx=αx\beta_{x}=\alpha_{x} is considered, and to the original KMP work [KMP82], corresponding to the full-refresh update with βx=∞\beta_{x}=\infty. We return to these cases and further possible generalizations in Remark 6.5 below.

For every k≥0k\geq 0, let 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k} denote the finite-dimensional space of polynomials of degree at most kk in the variables η∈Ωbd\eta\in\Omega_{\rm bd}; when restricting to Ω⊆Ωbd\Omega\subseteq\Omega_{\rm bd}, 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k} returns 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} from Section 1.1. It follows directly from the update rules that

(1.65) ℒbd​𝒬k⊆𝒬k​,k≥0​.\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}\mathscr{Q}_{k}\subseteq\mathscr{Q}_{k}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 0\,\text{.}

Indeed, the conservative updates preserve polynomial degree (cf. (1.10)), while a reservoir update (1.60)–(1.61) maps a polynomial of degree at most kk into another polynomial of either equal or lower degree. Hence, the restriction of ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} to 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k} is a finite-dimensional operator and admits polynomial eigenfunctions.

When ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} is self-adjoint, the invariance in (1.65) also yields the invariance of the orthogonal polynomial layers

(1.66) 𝒬k,∗≔𝒬k∩𝒬k−1⟂ν,k≥1.\mathscr{Q}_{k,\ast}\coloneqq\mathscr{Q}_{k}\cap\mathscr{Q}_{k-1}^{\perp_{\nu}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 1\,\text{.}

Together with the density of polynomials in L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu), this allows one to fully recover the L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu) spectrum from polynomial eigenfunctions. This argument breaks down in nonequilibrium. Indeed, although 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k} remains invariant, the orthogonal layer 𝒬k,∗\mathscr{Q}_{k,\ast} need not be invariant. Moreover, the restriction of ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} to 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k} need not be self-adjoint or even diagonalizable, and its eigenvalues need not exhaust the spectrum of ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} on L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu).

Regardless of this issue, one may always consider the polynomial spectrum spec⁡(−ℒbd|𝒬){\rm spec}(-\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}|_{\mathscr{Q}}), 𝒬≔∪k≥0𝒬k\mathscr{Q}\coloneqq\cup_{k\geq 0}\,\mathscr{Q}_{k}, defined as the collection of all eigenvalues of ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} on 𝒬\mathscr{Q}, counted with multiplicity. We shall prove that this spectrum is real, nonnegative and independent of ρ\rho. Accordingly, we define the polynomial spectral gap by

(1.67) gap⁡(ℒbd)≔infk≥1gap⁡(ℒbd|𝒬k)​,{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd})\coloneqq\inf_{k\geq 1}{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}|_{\mathscr{Q}_{k}})\;\text{,}\;\;

where gap⁡(ℒbd|𝒬k){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}|_{\mathscr{Q}_{k}}) denotes the second smallest eigenvalue of −ℒbd|𝒬k-\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}|_{\mathscr{Q}_{k}}. In the reversible case, gap⁡(ℒbd){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}) coincides with the usual L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu)-spectral gap. Our main finding is that, in contrast with the conservative setting of Theorem 1.1, this gap is always attained by a polynomial of degree one.

Theorem 1.11 (Boundary-driven KMP).

For all positive weights α,β,ρ\alpha,\beta,\rho and all non-negative weights ww and ω\omega, one has

(1.68) gap⁡(ℒbd)=gap⁡(ℒbd|𝒬1)​.{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd})={\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}|_{\mathscr{Q}_{1}})\,\text{.}

In particular, gap⁡(ℒbd){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}) does not depend on ρ\rho.

As in the conservative case, this result admits a particle-system interpretation: the relevant intertwining now involves the particle dynamics from Section 1.1.2 with an additional killing of particles at reservoir sites. We refer to Section 6 for further details.

1.3.3. Stochastic exchange models

The arguments used to prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 for the conservative KMP{\rm KMP} model extend to a considerably broader class of processes, which we refer to as stochastic exchange models; see also [KQS25, CQS25, CKMP25]. Roughly speaking, these are Markov processes on Ω\Omega whose updates redistribute the energy through multiplication with random stochastic matrices.

More specifically, let Υ\Upsilon be a Borel measure on the space of row-stochastic matrices M=(Mx​y)x,y∈[n]∈[0,1]n×nM=(M_{xy})_{x,y\in[n]}\in[0,1]^{n\times n}. The dynamics on Ω\Omega is formally described, for f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}, by

(1.69) ℒΥ​f​(η)≔∫Υ⁡(𝑑M)​(f⁡(η​M)−f⁡(η))​,η∈Ω​.\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}f(\eta)\coloneqq\int\Upsilon({\rm d}M)\left(f(\eta M)-f(\eta)\right)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\eta\in\Omega\,\text{.}

Here, η​M\eta M denotes row-vector–matrix multiplication; in particular, η​M∈Ω\eta M\in\Omega whenever η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega. We defer the precise construction of stochastic exchange models and further properties to Section 7. For now, let us simply note that the KMP{\rm KMP} generator in (1.6) corresponds to (cf. (1.5))

(1.70) Υ=ΥKMP=∑B⊆[n]wB​Law​(KBU)​,U=(Ux)x∈B∼Dir⁡(αB)​,\Upsilon=\Upsilon^{\rm\scriptscriptstyle KMP}=\textstyle{\sum_{B\subseteq[n]}}\,w_{B}\,{\rm Law}(K_{B}^{U})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad U=(U_{x})_{x\in B}\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha^{B})\;\text{,}\;\;

where KBU∈ℝn×nK_{B}^{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is the random row-stochastic matrix such that, for every η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega,

(1.71) (η​KBU)x=η⁡(B)​Ux​,​x∈B​,(η​KBU)x=ηx​,​x∉B​.(\eta K_{B}^{U})_{x}=\eta(B)U_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;x\in B\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad(\eta K_{B}^{U})_{x}=\eta_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;x\notin B\,\text{.}

Observe that the B×BB\times B block of KBU∈ℝn×nK_{B}^{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} has identical rows, each equal to U=(Ux)x∈BU=(U_{x})_{x\in B}.

As further examples, we anticipate that suitable variants of the KMP{\rm KMP} redistribution law in (1.70) yield:

  • •

    the averaging process considered in [AL12, QS23], obtained by taking the redistribution vector to be deterministic, with Ux=αxα⁡(B)U_{x}=\frac{\alpha_{x}}{\alpha(B)} for x∈Bx\in B;

  • •

    a block version of the immediate exchange model introduced in [HP14], obtained by taking the rows of the B×BB\times B update block to be independent—rather than identical—Dirichlet vectors with suitable parameters; see Section 7.4.2.

In all these examples, Υ\Upsilon is finite, and the corresponding generator ℒΥ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} is bounded on 𝒞⁡(Ω)\mathcal{C}(\Omega), the space of continuous functions on Ω\Omega endowed with the uniform norm. There are, however, relevant models described by an infinite measure Υ\Upsilon, most notably the harmonic process [FG22]; see Section 7.4.3. Each of the examples just mentioned admits a Dirichlet distribution as a reversible measure; for the averaging process, this degenerates to a Dirac mass.

To encompass all the above examples, we always impose, as in [KQS25], the condition

(1.72) ∫Υ⁡(𝑑M)​Mx​y<∞​,for every​x,y∈[n]​,​x≠y​.\textstyle\int\Upsilon({\rm d}M)M_{xy}<\infty\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{for every}\ x,y\in[n]\;\text{,}\;\;x\neq y\,\text{.}

This guarantees that (1.69) generates a Feller process on Ω\Omega. By compactness, an invariant probability measure always exists (Remark 7.2), while Theorem 1.12 and Proposition 7.6 provide explicit equivalent criteria for its uniqueness.

One key common feature of all these stochastic exchange models is that, under (1.72), the linearity of the updates in (1.69) guarantees

(1.73) ℒΥ​𝒫k⊆𝒫k​,k≥0​,\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}\mathscr{P}_{k}\subseteq\mathscr{P}_{k}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 0\;\text{,}\;\;

where 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} is the same space introduced in Section 1.1, namely, the space of polynomials of degree at most kk in the variables η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega. As in the preceding discussion on the boundary-driven KMP{\rm KMP} model, the eigenvalues obtained by diagonalizing ℒΥ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} on the finite-dimensional spaces 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} need not be in one-to-one correspondence with the spectrum of any L2L^{2} realization of the generator. Nevertheless, we may define the polynomial spectral gap by

(1.74) gap⁡(ℒΥ)≔infk≥1gap⁡(ℒΥ|𝒫k)​,{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon})\coloneqq\inf_{k\geq 1}{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}|_{\mathscr{P}_{k}})\;\text{,}\;\;

where gap⁡(ℒΥ|𝒫k){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}|_{\mathscr{P}_{k}}) is the smallest real part among the eigenvalues of −ℒΥ|𝒫k-\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}|_{\mathscr{P}_{k}} after removing one copy of the zero eigenvalue corresponding to constant functions, with algebraic multiplicities taken into account. With these definitions, the degree-two reduction established for the KMP{\rm KMP} model in Theorem 1.1 in fact holds throughout the whole class of stochastic exchange models.

Theorem 1.12 (Stochastic exchange models).

For every Borel measure Υ\Upsilon satisfying (1.72),

(1.75) gap⁡(ℒΥ)=gap⁡(ℒΥ|𝒫2)​.{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon})={\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}|_{\mathscr{P}_{2}})\,\text{.}

Moreover, ℒΥ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} admits a unique invariant measure precisely when gap⁡(ℒΥ)>0{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon})>0.

We stated the above result for restrictions to polynomial observables. If, in addition, the process is reversible with respect to a probability measure which is absolutely continuous with respect to the uniform measure on Ω\Omega, then distinct polynomial functions on Ω\Omega define distinct elements of the corresponding L2L^{2}-space. Since polynomials are dense in this space, self-adjointness yields a complete orthonormal basis of polynomial eigenfunctions. Consequently, gap⁡(ℒΥ){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}) coincides with the usual L2L^{2}-spectral gap. This applies, in particular, whenever the reversible measure is a nondegenerate Dirichlet distribution, thus, to the immediate exchange model and harmonic process; see Corollaries 7.9 and 7.11.

We provide further motivation for this general spectral gap reduction in the next section, where we outline the key steps of its proof.

1.4. Hidden models, proof strategy, and further remarks

As for the KMP{\rm KMP} model, every stochastic exchange model as introduced in Section 1.3.3 admits a natural particle representation. Consequently, the spectral problems for polynomial eigenfunctions underlying Theorem 1.1 and its extension in Theorem 1.12 can be equivalently reformulated in terms of eigenpairs of the associated finite-particle systems; see (7.30). The most effective viewpoint for proving the degree-two reductions in those theorems, however, comes from a different representation: the hidden (temperature or parameter) model, first identified for KMP{\rm KMP} in [DMFG24]; see also [GRT25, KQS25] for subsequent developments and extensions.

1.4.1. Hidden models

To introduce the hidden model in an intuitive way, first observe that the KMP{\rm KMP} model—as any other stochastic exchange model with generator ℒΥ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} as in (1.69)—is built from elementary random matrix updates of the form

(1.76) η⟼η​M​,\eta\longmapsto\eta M\;\text{,}\;\;

where η∈Ω⊆ℝn\eta\in\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, viewed as a row vector, is a probability distribution on [n][n], and M∈ℝn×nM\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is row-stochastic. For instance, the KMP{\rm KMP} update in (1.2), restricted to the coordinates x,y=x+1∈[n]x,y=x+1\in[n] (as the others remain unchanged), can be written as

(1.77) (ηx,ηy)⟼(ηx,ηy)​(U1−UU1−U)=(U⁡(ηx+ηy),(1−U)​(ηx+ηy))​.(\eta_{x},\eta_{y})\longmapsto(\eta_{x},\eta_{y})\begin{pmatrix}U&1-U\\ U&1-U\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}U(\eta_{x}+\eta_{y}),(1-U)(\eta_{x}+\eta_{y})\end{pmatrix}\,\text{.}

Hence, at any time t>0t>0, after ℓ=ℓ⁡(t)\ell=\ell(t) updates (1.76) with matrices M1,…,MℓM_{1},\ldots,M_{\ell}, the energy configuration is ηM1⋯Mℓ\eta M_{1}\cdots M_{\ell}. Crucially, the update times and matrices are sampled independently of the current energy configuration. The same sequence may therefore be read in reverse chronological order and applied, by left multiplication, to a column vector, still yielding a Markov dynamics.

This backward evolution is precisely the hidden model: its configurations are column vectors θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and each update takes the form

(1.78) θ⟼M​θ​,\theta\longmapsto M\theta\;\text{,}\;\;

so that the same row-stochastic matrix MM now acts on the hidden-model configuration from the left. In particular, the matrix representation of the KMP{\rm KMP} update in (1.77) gives the corresponding θ\theta-variable update

(1.79) (θxθy)⟼(U1−UU1−U)​(θxθy)=(U​θx+(1−U)​θyU​θx+(1−U)​θy)​.\begin{pmatrix}\theta_{x}\\ \theta_{y}\end{pmatrix}\longmapsto\begin{pmatrix}U&1-U\\ U&1-U\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\theta_{x}\\ \theta_{y}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}U\theta_{x}+(1-U)\theta_{y}\\ U\theta_{x}+(1-U)\theta_{y}\end{pmatrix}\,\text{.}

Observe that, whereas the forward update in (1.77) redistributes the conserved total energy ηx+ηy\eta_{x}+\eta_{y} between the two sites, the hidden-model update in (1.79) replaces θx\theta_{x} and θy\theta_{y} by the same random convex combination and, in general, does not preserve their sum. The same description extends to the KMP{\rm KMP} hidden model on a weighted hypergraph: whenever a block is updated, all its coordinates are replaced by a common random convex combination. Thus, for the KMP{\rm KMP} hidden-model dynamics,

  1. (1)

    every flat configuration s​𝟏s\mathbf{1}, s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, is invariant;

  2. (2)

    the minimum coordinate is nondecreasing and the maximum coordinate is nonincreasing, so every hypercube [a,b]n[a,b]^{n}, −∞<a<b<∞-\infty<a<b<\infty, is invariant;

  3. (3)

    the total mass need not be conserved.

The properties in 1–3 are not specific to the hidden model of the KMP{\rm KMP}, but are shared by the hidden model of any stochastic exchange model from Section 1.3.3. Indeed, every row-stochastic matrix MM satisfies M​𝟏=𝟏M\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1} and each coordinate of M​θM\theta is a convex combination of the coordinates of θ\theta, yielding respectively the invariance of flat configurations in 1 and the maximum principle in 2. Moreover, in general,

(1.80) ∑x∈[n](M​θ)x≠∑x∈[n]θx​,\textstyle\sum_{x\in[n]}(M\theta)_{x}\neq\sum_{x\in[n]}\theta_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;

so the hidden-model dynamics is typically non-conservative, i.e., 3.

Under an appropriate connectivity assumption, the hidden-model dynamics converges, in the long run, to a flat configuration with a possibly random height. Although the degeneracy of these steady states may at first appear as a complication, it is precisely what makes the hidden-model representation effective for the spectral gap problem.

1.4.2. Eigenvalue problem for hidden models

The original KMP{\rm KMP} model, its particle representation, and its hidden model all encode the same polynomial eigenvalue problem. Indeed, for given weights α=(αx)x∈[n]\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in[n]} and w=(wB)B⊆[n]w=(w_{B})_{B\subseteq[n]}, k≥1k\geq 1, and ψ∈ℋk\psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k} as defined in (1.19), next to the η\eta-variable polynomial ψ^∈𝒫k\widehat{\psi}\in\mathscr{P}_{k} introduced in (1.13), we also define

(1.81) ψ~(θ)≔∑x1,…,xk∈[n]μk(x1,…,xk)ψ(x1,…,xk)θx1⋯θxk,θ∈ℝn,\widetilde{\psi}(\theta)\coloneqq\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in[n]}\mu_{k}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\theta_{x_{1}}\cdots\theta_{x_{k}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;\text{,}\;\;

where μk\mu_{k} is the reversible measure of the kk-particle system; see (1.17). Comparing ψ~\widetilde{\psi} in (1.81) with ψ^\widehat{\psi} in (1.13), the two polynomials differ only by the additional coefficient μk​(x1,…,xk)\mu_{k}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) attached to each monomial.

Recall that ℒ\mathcal{L} denotes the generator of the (α,w)(\alpha,w)-KMP{\rm KMP} model, while LkL_{k} is the generator of the associated kk-particle system. As seen in (1.14), the map ψ↦ψ^\psi\mapsto\widehat{\psi} on ℋk\mathscr{H}_{k} intertwines these two generators; the map ψ↦ψ~\psi\mapsto\widetilde{\psi} in (1.81) yields the corresponding relation with the hidden-model dynamics. More precisely, if ℒ\mathscr{L} denotes the generator of the hidden model, then

(1.82) ℒ​ψ^=Lk​ψ^andℒ​ψ~=Lk​ψ~​,for every​ψ∈ℋk​.\mathcal{L}\widehat{\psi}=\widehat{L_{k}\psi}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathscr{L}\widetilde{\psi}=\widetilde{L_{k}\psi}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{for every}\ \psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k}\,\text{.}

In view of these intertwining relations, we shall prove that, for every λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and ψ∈ℋk\psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k},

(1.83) ℒψ^=−λψ^⟺Lkψ=−λψ⟺ℒψ~=−λψ~.\mathcal{L}\widehat{\psi}=-\lambda\widehat{\psi}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad L_{k}\psi=-\lambda\psi\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\mathscr{L}\widetilde{\psi}=-\lambda\widetilde{\psi}\,\text{.}

Since ψ\psi, ψ^\widehat{\psi}, and ψ~\widetilde{\psi} may only vanish simultaneously, the eigenvalue problem may be formulated interchangeably for the KMP{\rm KMP} generator, the kk-particle system on symmetric observables, or the hidden model.

In view of the degeneracy of the hidden model steady states, the last formulation in (1.83) has the advantage of translating the problem of identifying the optimal L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu) convergence rate of the KMP{\rm KMP} dynamics toward its Dirichlet equilibrium, as in (1.8), into the more tractable task of quantifying the decay of spatial fluctuations in the hidden model.

A natural first candidate for measuring spatial fluctuations of the hidden-model profile is the variance with respect to the probability measure induced by α=(αx)x∈[n]\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in[n]}. More precisely, for x∈[n]x\in[n] and θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, set

(1.84) πx≔αxα0​,π⁡(θ)≔∑x∈[n]πx​θx​,Varπ​(θ)≔∑x∈[n]πx​(θx−π⁡(θ))2​.\textstyle\pi_{x}\coloneqq\frac{\alpha_{x}}{\alpha_{0}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\pi(\theta)\coloneqq\sum_{x\in[n]}\pi_{x}\,\theta_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad{\rm Var}_{\pi}(\theta)\coloneqq\sum_{x\in[n]}\pi_{x}\left(\theta_{x}-\pi(\theta)\right)^{2}\,\text{.}

1.4.4. A Perron-Frobenius theorem for nonnegative quadratic functions

The preceding argument does not allow, in general, to prove that the optimal variance-contraction rate δ⁡(α,w)\delta(\alpha,w) in (1.85) always coincides with gap2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w). A closer inspection, though, shows that this identity does hold in some instances, namely, in homogeneous mean-field settings, such as

(1.93) α≡const.,​wB=𝟙|B|=ℓ​,for some​ℓ=2,…,n−1​.\textstyle\alpha\equiv{\rm const.}\;\text{,}\;\;w_{B}=\mathds{1}_{{|B|=\ell}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{for some}\ \ell=2,\ldots,n-1\,\text{.}

Indeed, in this case all the inequalities in (1.87) become identities (Remark 5.9), yielding

(1.94) ℒ​Varπ=−γ⁡(α,w)​gap1​(α,w)​Varπ​.\mathscr{L}{\rm Var}_{\pi}=-\gamma(\alpha,w)\,{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)\,{\rm Var}_{\pi}\,\text{.}

Thus, in this context, Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} is itself an eigenfunction of −ℒ-\mathscr{L} with eigenvalue γ⁡(α,w)​gap1​(α,w)\gamma(\alpha,w)\,{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w), which necessarily coincides with δ⁡(α,w)\delta(\alpha,w) in (1.85). Moreover, Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} is a nonzero, quadratic polynomial in the θ\theta-variables that vanishes precisely on constant configurations. Leveraging on the correspondence in (1.83), one then proves that Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} is a genuine degree-two eigenfunction, so that gap2,∗​(α,w)≤γ⁡(α,w)​gap1​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w)\leq\gamma(\alpha,w)\,{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w). Combined with (1.89) for k=2k=2, this forces

(1.95) γ⁡(α,w)​gap1​(α,w)=δ⁡(α,w)=gap2,∗​(α,w)​.\gamma(\alpha,w)\,{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)=\delta(\alpha,w)={\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w)\,\text{.}

Hence, in the homogeneous mean-field setting (1.93), one obtains not only

(1.96) infk≥2gapk,∗​(α,w)=gap2,∗​(α,w)​,\inf_{k\geq 2}{\rm gap}_{k,\ast}(\alpha,w)={\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w)\;\text{,}\;\;

but also the stronger structural fact that Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} is a nonnegative quadratic eigenfunction of −ℒ-\mathscr{L} associated with gap2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w) and vanishing precisely on flat configurations. These are exactly the properties used in the preceding argument: nonnegativity and quadratic vanishing yield the pointwise domination in (1.90), while the eigenvalue equation provides the sharp decay rate gap2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w), rather than merely a computable lower bound.

For general geometries, Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} is typically no longer an eigenfunction. The central finding of our approach is that the properties above can nevertheless always be recovered simultaneously for any KMP{\rm KMP} hidden-model dynamics: for all positive site weights α\alpha and nonnegative block weights ww, under suitable irreducibility assumptions there exists a nonzero quadratic function g∗≥0g_{\ast}\geq 0, strictly positive away from flat configurations, such that

(1.97) ℒ​g∗=−gap2,∗​(α,w)​g∗​.\mathscr{L}g_{\ast}=-{\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w)\,g_{\ast}\,\text{.}

Thus, g∗g_{\ast} may replace Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} as a Lyapunov function in (1.91), while capturing the optimal rate; cf. (3.14).

Let us emphasize that the existence of such a one-signed eigenfunction is a distinctive feature of the absorbing hidden-model dynamics. Every nonconstant eigenfunction of the original KMP{\rm KMP} generator associated with a nonzero eigenvalue is orthogonal to constants in L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu) and must therefore change sign. In the hidden-model variables, instead, in view of the degenerate form of its steady state, the corresponding eigenfunction may be nonnegative, vanishing on the absorbing family of flat configurations.

Ultimately, the key step is therefore to establish the existence of such a distinguished eigenfunction g∗g_{\ast}. Once the appropriate functional setting has been identified, this existence result follows rather directly from Perron–Frobenius theorems applied on suitable cones of nonnegative quadratic hidden-model observables. Although the underlying tool is classical, its application to degree-two polynomials in the hidden-model variables appears to be both novel and rather unexpected. It is also remarkably powerful: the resulting eigenfunction encodes substantial structural information, which we exploit systematically in the proofs of the characterization theorems in Section 1.2. Finally, this same mechanism proves to be quite universal, extending beyond the KMP{\rm KMP} model to all stochastic exchange models.

1.4.5. Further remarks and results

In fact, although the proof sketch above captures the essence of our approach, a Perron–Frobenius theorem as described there—and, in fact, the stronger version established in Proposition 3.5—plays a key role only in the finer comparison results from Section 1.2. For the proofs of Theorems 1.1–1.2 and of their stochastic-exchange-model counterpart, Theorem 1.12, it suffices instead to exhibit a suitable quadratic nonnegative and nondegenerate—in the sense of (3.3)—polynomial, not necessarily an eigenfunction of the generator. A convenient choice for such a polynomial is the variance functional Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} from (1.84).

This more general principle also yields refined information on higher-degree spectral gaps. Indeed, at every even degree ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, the same role is played by the homogeneous polynomial Varπℓ/2{\rm Var}_{\pi}^{\ell/2}, yielding gapk,∗​(α,w)≥gapk−1,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{k,\ast}(\alpha,w)\geq{\rm gap}_{k-1,\ast}(\alpha,w) for odd k≥3k\geq 3 and gapk,∗​(α,w)≥gapk−2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{k,\ast}(\alpha,w)\geq{\rm gap}_{k-2,\ast}(\alpha,w) for even k≥4k\geq 4. See Remarks 2.10 and 3.10, as well as Remark 7.4 for the analogous statement for stochastic exchange models. In particular, when α≡1\alpha\equiv 1, the monotonicity along even degrees in (2.71) proves another conjecture raised by Alon and Puder in [AP26], namely, part of [AP26, Conjecture 4.16].

1.4.6. Open problems

As already discussed at the beginning of Section 1, Aldous-type spectral gap phenomena have by now been identified both for classical interacting particle systems and for stochastic dynamics on groups, creating links between statistical and quantum physics, combinatorics, group theory, and representation theory; see, e.g., [Ces16, HS19, QS23, BC24, KS24, AKP25, AP26, LP26, GZ26, Zhu26] and references therein. All previously known results and conjectures associated with the symmetric group and its variants can be interpreted, in the corresponding particle or energy variables, as degree-one spectral gap reductions. A prominent open problem in this direction is Caputo’s conjecture for the interchange process on arbitrary weighted hypergraphs; see Remark 7.8. Another related important open problem is the general degree-two reduction conjectured by Alon and Puder for the unitary group, see [AP26, Conjecture 1.7]. Our results provide the first proof of general degree-two spectral gap reductions on arbitrary geometries for a broad class of stochastic exchange dynamics. Finding further occurrences of this phenomenon, and identifying a common mechanism behind them, remains an interesting open problem.

A natural test case is the Brownian energy process (BEP{\rm BEP}), another conservative stochastic dynamics of energies on a weighted nn-site graph, parametrized by site weights α\alpha and edge weights ww as the KMP{\rm KMP} model, but evolving diffusively rather than through random exchange updates. On Ω\Omega, it is reversible with respect to μ=Dir⁡(α)\mu={\rm Dir}(\alpha) and has generator

(1.98) ℒBEPf(η)=12∑x,y∈[n]w{x,y}{−(αyηx−αxηy)(∂ηx−∂ηy)+ηxηy(∂ηx−∂ηy)2}f(η).\mathcal{L}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle BEP}}f(\eta)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in[n]}w_{\left\{x,y\right\}}\left\{-\left(\alpha_{y}\eta_{x}-\alpha_{x}\eta_{y}\right)\left(\partial_{\eta_{x}}-\partial_{\eta_{y}}\right)+\eta_{x}\eta_{y}\left(\partial_{\eta_{x}}-\partial_{\eta_{y}}\right)^{2}\right\}f(\eta)\,\text{.}

As for the stochastic exchange models above, ℒBEP\mathcal{L}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle BEP}} preserves polynomial degree and is intertwined with a particle system, known as the symmetric inclusion process (SIP{\rm SIP}). The results of [KS24, KS26] establish one-particle domination when minx∈[n]⁡αx≥1\min_{x\in[n]}\alpha_{x}\geq 1, show that it may fail outside this regime, and prove an asymptotic two-particle reduction under the rescaling α↦τ​α\alpha\mapsto\tau\alpha as τ→0\tau\to 0. Whether, for arbitrary weighted graphs and positive site weights, the spectral gap is always attained at degree at most two remains open.

Our hidden-model approach does not seem to extend directly to this problem. The formal hidden-model operator would read

(1.99) ℒBEPg(θ)=12∑x,y∈[n]w{x,y}{−(θx−θy)(αy∂θx−αx∂θy)+(θx−θy)2∂θx∂θy}g(θ).\mathscr{L}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle BEP}}g(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in[n]}w_{\left\{x,y\right\}}\left\{-\left(\theta_{x}-\theta_{y}\right)\left(\alpha_{y}\partial_{\theta_{x}}-\alpha_{x}\partial_{\theta_{y}}\right)+\left(\theta_{x}-\theta_{y}\right)^{2}\partial_{\theta_{x}}\partial_{\theta_{y}}\right\}g(\theta)\,\text{.}

but this operator is not Markovian. Indeed, if w{x,y}>0w_{\left\{x,y\right\}}>0 and c≠0c\neq 0, then g⁡(θ)=(θx−θy−c)2g(\theta)=(\theta_{x}-\theta_{y}-c)^{2} attains its minimum whenever θx−θy=c\theta_{x}-\theta_{y}=c, while ℒBEP​g​(θ)=−2​w{x,y}​c2<0\mathscr{L}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle BEP}}g(\theta)=-2w_{\left\{x,y\right\}}c^{2}<0 there, violating the positive minimum principle. Thus, even in this closely related diffusion setting, a proof of the conjectural degree-two reduction appears to require a different mechanism.

Organization of the paper

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 is devoted to the proof of Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Theorem 1.10. Section 3 develops the Perron–Frobenius theory used in the comparison between one- and two-particle gaps. Section 4 reduces this comparison to minimal hypergraphs, while Section 5 completes the proofs of the results stated in Section 1.2. Section 6 treats the boundary-driven KMP{\rm KMP} model and proves Theorem 1.11. Finally, Section 7 develops the general theory of stochastic exchange models, proves Theorem 1.12, and discusses several examples. The appendix contains the refinement needed in the analysis of minimal hypergraphs. Sections 2.3 and 6 may each be read independently of the remaining sections.

2. Aldous’ phenomenon in KMP{\rm KMP}

The main goal of this section is to prove Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.10. We start by presenting all definitions, properties and intertwining relations involving the KMP{\rm KMP} model, the corresponding particle system, and its hidden model. We then turn to the proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 in Section 2.2. Finally, in Section 2.3 we show how a mild extension of these results leads to the statement for Gibbs samplers on cone measures from Theorem 1.10.

2.1. Energies, particles, hidden models, and intertwining relations

We now make precise the three equivalent formulations of the polynomial spectral problem announced in (1.83). For this purpose, we first describe the KMP{\rm KMP} dynamics, its labeled-particle representation, and the corresponding hidden model. Then, we identify the polynomial spaces on which the three generators are intertwined. The positive site weights α\alpha and nonnegative block weights ww are fixed throughout the section, without imposing any additional assumption. For every integer k≥1k\geq 1, we shall use the shorthand notation

(2.1) ℋk⊗≔ℝ[n]k={ψ:[n]k→ℝ}​,\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{[n]^{k}}=\{\psi:[n]^{k}\to\mathbb{R}\}\;\text{,}\;\;

and write L2​(μk)L^{2}(\mu_{k}) when endowing ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} with the μk\mu_{k}-inner product. Further, recall that ℋk⊆ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k}\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}, defined in (1.19), is its subspace of symmetric functions.

2.1.1. KMP, particle, and hidden models

while those outside BB remain unchanged. Hence, its generator acts on continuous functions g:ℝn→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} as

For the labeled-particle formulation, it is useful to introduce synchronized kk-copy versions of the KMP{\rm KMP} energy and hidden-model dynamics. By synchronized, we mean that all kk copies undergo each update simultaneously, using the same block BB and the same redistribution vector UU. Proposition 2.2.

For every k≥1k\geq 1, the maps in (2.13) are linear isomorphisms

Proposition 2.3 (Intertwining relations).

For every k≥1k\geq 1 and ψ∈ℋk⊗\psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes},

(2.23) ℒk⊗​ψ^⊗=Lk​ψ^⊗​,ℒk⊗​ψ~⊗=Lk​ψ~⊗​.\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\widehat{\psi}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}=\widehat{L_{k}\psi}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathscr{L}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\widetilde{\psi}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}=\widetilde{L_{k}\psi}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\,\text{.}

Fix a block B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n]. For the hat map in (2.11) and (2.15), right multiplication gives, conditionally on UU and for all η(1),…,η(k)∈Ω\eta^{(1)},\ldots,\eta^{(k)}\in\Omega,

For the tilde map in (2.12) and (2.16), left multiplication gives, for all θ(1),…,θ(k)∈ℝn\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

(2.26) 𝐄B[ψ~⊗(KBUθ(1),…,KBUθ(k))]=∑x1,…,xk∈[n]μk(x1,…,xk)(ΠB,kψ)(x1,…,xk)θx1(1)⋯θxk(k),\displaystyle\mathbf{E}_{B}[\widetilde{\psi}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}(K_{B}^{U}\theta^{(1)},\ldots,K_{B}^{U}\theta^{(k)})]=\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in[n]}\mu_{k}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,(\Pi_{B,k}\psi)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\theta_{x_{1}}^{(1)}\cdots\theta_{x_{k}}^{(k)}\;\text{,}\;\;

where we used that the heat-bath operator ΠB,k\Pi_{B,k} given in (2.5) is self-adjoint on L2​(μk)L^{2}(\mu_{k}). This gives the second identity in (2.23).

The diagonal configurations η(1)=⋯=η(k)\eta^{(1)}=\cdots=\eta^{(k)} and θ(1)=…=θ(k)\theta^{(1)}=\ldots=\theta^{(k)} are both preserved by every synchronous update. Moreover, the restrictions of ℒk⊗\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} and ℒk⊗\mathscr{L}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} to the diagonal coincide with ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℒ\mathscr{L}, respectively. Since LkL_{k} preserves ℋk\mathscr{H}_{k}, the identities in (2.24) follow. ∎

By Proposition 2.2, the intertwinings in Proposition 2.3 establish the equivalence (1.83), and induce similarity relations between finite-dimensional projections of the generators. Consequently, one obtains, counting multiplicities,

(2.27) spec⁡(ℒ|𝒫k)=spec⁡(Lksym)=spec⁡(ℒ|ℛk)​,{\rm spec}(\mathcal{L}|_{\mathscr{P}_{k}})={\rm spec}(L_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}})={\rm spec}(\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{R}_{k}})\;\text{,}\;\;

We conclude this part with a simple observation establishing (1.9).

Remark 2.4.

For fixed weights α\alpha and ww, the LkL_{k}-particle system and the system of kk independent and labeled L1L_{1}-particles not only share the same state space [n]k[n]^{k}, but also the same communicating classes. Indeed, whenever wB>0w_{B}>0, both dynamics allow any single particle to move alone between sites of BB with positive rate, while not allowing any particles to leave a connected component of the ww-hypergraph. Thus, if the latter has mm connected components, the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of LkL_{k} (resp. LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}}) is mkm^{k} (resp. (k+m−1m−1)\binom{k+m-1}{m-1}). In particular, LkL_{k} and LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} have a simple zero eigenvalue if and only if m=1m=1, namely, when the ww-hypergraph is connected. By (2.27)–(2.28) and (1.11), this proves (1.9).

For an alternative approach to (1.9), see [AP26] and, in particular, Section 5.2 therein.

2.1.3. Decomposition of polynomial spaces

In this section, we systematically describe the subspaces 𝒫k,∗⊆𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k,\ast}\subseteq\mathscr{P}_{k} introduced in (1.27), together with their particle-system and hidden-model counterparts. The resulting decompositions will be instrumental in identifying the eigenfunctions genuinely arising at degree kk. In view of Proposition 2.2, it is natural to start from the spaces of polynomial coefficients, thus, from the particle system.

Fix k≥1k\geq 1, and recall ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} and ℋk\mathscr{H}_{k} from (2.1) and (1.19), respectively. For every i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k, define the particle-removal and particle-addition operators acting on ϕ∈ℋk−1⊗\phi\in\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} and ψ∈ℋk⊗\psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}, respectively, as

(2.29) 𝔞k,i​ϕ​(x1,…,xk)≔ϕ⁡(x1,…,xi−1,xi+1,…,xk)​,x1,…,xk∈[n]​,\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}\phi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\coloneqq\phi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{k})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in[n]\;\text{,}\;\;
(2.30) 𝔟k−1,i​ψ​(x1,…,xk−1)≔∑y∈[n]μk​(y∣x1,…,xk−1)​ψ​(x1,…,xi−1,y,xi,…,xk−1)​,\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i}\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1})\coloneqq\sum_{y\in[n]}\mu_{k}(y\mid x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1})\,\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1},y,x_{i},\ldots,x_{k-1})\;\text{,}\;\;

where μk​(y∣x1,…,xk−1)≔μk​(x1,…,xk−1,y)μk−1​(x1,…,xk−1)\mu_{k}(y\mid x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1})\coloneqq\frac{\mu_{k}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1},y)}{\mu_{k-1}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1})}; see (1.17). Thus,

(2.31) 𝔞k,i:ℋk−1⊗→ℋk⊗​,𝔟k−1,i:ℋk⊗→ℋk−1⊗​,\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}:\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\to\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i}:\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\to\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\;\text{,}\;\;

and, as their names suggest, both 𝔞k,i\mathfrak{a}_{k,i} and 𝔟k−1,i\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i} are stochastic operators between particle configuration spaces, with a transparent probabilistic interpretation: the former induces a deterministic removal of the ii-th particle, whereas the latter adds a particle whose position is averaged over its conditional equilibrium distribution given the positions of all remaining particles.

A simple computation shows that these operators are adjoint of one another, namely,

(2.32) ⟨𝔞k,i​ϕ,ψ⟩μk=⟨ϕ,𝔟k−1,i​ψ⟩μk−1​,ϕ∈ℋk−1⊗​,​ψ∈ℋk⊗​.\left\langle\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}\phi,\psi\right\rangle_{\mu_{k}}=\left\langle\phi,\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i}\psi\right\rangle_{\mu_{k-1}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\phi\in\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\;\text{,}\;\;\psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\,\text{.}

As 𝔞k,i\mathfrak{a}_{k,i} is clearly injective, this ensures that 𝔟k−1,i\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i} is surjective.

The tensor form of the matrix update in (2.5) gives

(2.33) (KBU)⊗k​𝔞k,i=𝔞k,i​(KBU)⊗(k−1)​.(K_{B}^{U})^{\otimes k}\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}=\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}(K_{B}^{U})^{\otimes(k-1)}\,\text{.}

Combining this with (2.4) and (2.32) yields, respectively,

(2.34) Lk​𝔞k,i=𝔞k,i​Lk−1​,𝔟k−1,i​Lk=Lk−1​𝔟k−1,i​.L_{k}\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}=\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}L_{k-1}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i}L_{k}=L_{k-1}\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i}\,\text{.}

The first relation in (2.34) is sometimes referred to as the consistency of the particle system: evolving kk particles and then removing the ii-th one yields the same law as first removing that particle and then evolving the remaining k−1k-1 particles.

Next, we introduce the symmetrized operators

(2.35) 𝔞k≔1k​∑i=1k𝔞k,i​,𝔟k−1≔1k​∑i=1k𝔟k−1,i​,\textstyle\mathfrak{a}_{k}\coloneqq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathfrak{b}_{k-1}\coloneqq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i}\;\text{,}\;\;

which admit the analogous interpretation of removing or adding a particle, whose label is now chosen uniformly at random. Moreover, one has

(2.36) 𝔞k​(ℋk−1)⊆ℋk​,𝔟k−1​(ℋk)=ℋk−1​,\mathfrak{a}_{k}(\mathscr{H}_{k-1})\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{k}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathfrak{b}_{k-1}(\mathscr{H}_{k})=\mathscr{H}_{k-1}\;\text{,}\;\;

and it is not difficult to check that the restriction 𝔞k|ℋk−1\mathfrak{a}_{k}|_{\mathscr{H}_{k-1}} is injective; see [KS24, Lemma A.2]. Finally, by linearity, 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} and 𝔟k−1\mathfrak{b}_{k-1} satisfy commutation relations analogous to those in (2.34).

The first identity in (2.34), its symmetrized counterpart, and the aforementioned injectivity of the particle-removal operators show that lower-level eigenfunctions may be canonically lifted. More precisely, if 0≠ϕ∈ℋk−10\neq\phi\in\mathscr{H}_{k-1} is an eigenfunction of Lk−1symL_{k-1}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} with eigenvalue λ\lambda, then 0≠𝔞k​ϕ∈ℋk0\neq\mathfrak{a}_{k}\phi\in\mathscr{H}_{k} is an eigenfunction of LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} with the same eigenvalue; likewise, 0≠𝔞k,i​ϕ∈ℋk⊗0\neq\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}\phi\in\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}, i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k, is an eigenfunction of LkL_{k} whenever 0≠ϕ∈ℋk−1⊗0\neq\phi\in\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} is an eigenfunction of Lk−1L_{k-1}. Injectivity of 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} and 𝔞k,i\mathfrak{a}_{k,i} ensures that these liftings are nontrivial. Thus, the images of the removal operators contain no genuinely new eigenpairs. Since LksymL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}} and LkL_{k} are self-adjoint, the orthogonal complement of these images are invariant and indicate the natural spaces in which to search for new eigenfunctions. Letting ℋk,∗⊆ℋk\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast}\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{k} and ℋk,∗⊗⊆ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} denote such complements, one obtains the following orthogonal decompositions

(2.37) ℋk=𝔞k(ℋk−1)⊕μkℋk,∗,ℋk⊗=(𝔞k,1(ℋk−1⊗)+⋯+𝔞k,k(ℋk−1⊗))⊕μkℋk,∗⊗.\textstyle\mathscr{H}_{k}=\mathfrak{a}_{k}(\mathscr{H}_{k-1})\oplus_{\mu_{k}}\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}=\big(\mathfrak{a}_{k,1}(\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes})+\cdots+\mathfrak{a}_{k,k}(\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes})\big)\oplus_{\mu_{k}}\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\,\text{.}

Here, the symbol ⊕μk\oplus_{\mu_{k}} stands for a direct sum of μk\mu_{k}-orthogonal subspaces, whereas ++ indicates a (not necessarily direct) sum of the subspaces 𝔞k,i​(ℋk−1⊗)\mathfrak{a}_{k,i}(\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}), i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k.

In view of the above decompositions and of the adjointness relation (2.32), we find that such orthogonal complements may be expressed in terms of kernels of the addition operators.

Proposition 2.5.

The orthogonal complements in (2.37) are given by

(2.38) ℋk,∗=ker⁡(𝔟k−1|ℋk)⊆ℋk​,ℋk,∗⊗=⋂i=1kker⁡(𝔟k−1,i)⊆ℋk⊗​.\textstyle\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast}={\rm ker}(\mathfrak{b}_{k-1}|_{\mathscr{H}_{k}})\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{k}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}=\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}{\rm ker}(\mathfrak{b}_{k-1,i})\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}\,\text{.}

The spaces ℋk,∗\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast} and ℋk,∗⊗\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} consist precisely of the eigenfunctions that do not arise from ℋk−1\mathscr{H}_{k-1} and ℋk−1⊗\mathscr{H}_{k-1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}. By Proposition 2.2, the restrictions of the hat and tilde maps to these spaces are linear isomorphisms onto their respective images. The intertwining relations in Proposition 2.3 then imply that these images are invariant under the corresponding generators, and that the restricted maps identify their eigenfunctions bijectively while preserving the associated eigenvalues. Hence, our final task is to identify these images in the polynomial spaces of the KMP{\rm KMP} and its hidden model.

We start by recovering the η\eta-polynomials in (1.27).

Moreover, ∥⋅∥a,b\|\cdot\|_{a,b} is a norm on the finite-dimensional space ℛℓ,∗\mathscr{R}_{\ell,\ast}, and this space is invariant under ℒ\mathscr{L} by (2.43). Since G≠0G\neq 0, we may choose θ(1),…,θ(k)∈[a,b]n\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(k)}\in[a,b]^{n} such that G⁡(θ(1),…,θ(k))≠0G(\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(k)})\neq 0. As λ≥gapk,∗⊗​(α,w)\lambda\geq{\rm gap}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes}(\alpha,w), this proves, for every 2≤ℓ≤k2\leq\ell\leq k with ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 even,

Choosing ℓ=2\ell=2 proves (2.55) and, thus, concludes the proof. ∎
