3. Perron–Frobenius theorems on quadratic cones for KMP

In this section, we prepare the ground for establishing the main results described in Section 1.2, aimed at comparing gap1​(α,w){\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w) with gap2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w). As already announced in Section 1.4.4 and motivated by the role played by the variance functional Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} in (1.84), the key idea is to identify a nonnegative quadratic eigenfunction of the hidden model, and exploit the accompanying structural properties—most notably, its strict positivity and uniqueness, together with the analogous properties of the dual eigenfunction. These conclusions will follow from the Perron–Frobenius theory for cone-preserving operators—the finite-dimensional counterpart of the Krein–Rutman theorem—and its refinements. Although we focus on quadratic cones, some of our conclusions admit extensions to even-degree polynomials (Remark 3.10).

Throughout the section, the weights α\alpha and ww are fixed, while additional assumptions on them will be introduced when needed.

3.1. The quadratic cone and positivity

Our first task is to identify the appropriate setting for analyzing the eigenspace associated to gap2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w). In view of the linear isomorphisms intertwining the operators in (2.51), we focus, as already done in Section 2.2, on the restriction ℒ|ℛ2,∗\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{R}_{2,\ast}} of the hidden-model generator to the finite-dimensional space ℛ2,∗\mathscr{R}_{2,\ast} described in (2.44). For brevity, throughout this section we simply write

(3.1) ℛ≔ℛ2,∗​.\mathscr{R}\coloneqq\mathscr{R}_{2,\ast}\,\text{.}

Recall that every g∈ℛg\in\mathscr{R} is a homogeneous quadratic θ\theta-polynomial invariant under translations along 𝟏∈ℝn\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. In particular, since g∈ℛg\in\mathscr{R} satisfies g⁡(𝟎)=0g(\mathbf{0})=0, it must also vanish on constant configurations: g⁡(s​𝟏)=0g(s\mathbf{1})=0 for every s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}.

The natural subset in which to seek the desired eigenfunction is therefore

(3.2) 𝒞≔ℛ+={g∈ℛ:g⁡(θ)≥0​for every​θ∈ℝn}​.\mathscr{C}\coloneqq\mathscr{R}_{\scriptscriptstyle+}=\{g\in\mathscr{R}:g(\theta)\geq 0\ \text{for every}\ \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}\,\text{.}

Following the terminology in, e.g., [SV70, Definition 1] or [Hog14, §36.1], it is immediate to verify that 𝒞\mathscr{C} is a proper cone in ℛ\mathscr{R}. Indeed, it is closed and convex, stable under multiplication by nonnegative scalars, and pointed, since 𝒞∩(−𝒞)={0}\mathscr{C}\cap(-\mathscr{C})=\{0\}. Moreover, its interior

(3.3) int(𝒞)={g∈𝒞:g(θ)=0if and only ifθ=const.}{\rm int}(\mathscr{C})=\left\{g\in\mathscr{C}:g(\theta)=0\ \text{if and only if}\ \theta={\rm const.}\right\}

is nonempty as, for instance, Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} belongs to it; cf. Lemma 2.8 with k=2k=2. Here and below, interiors are taken in the finite-dimensional space ℛ\mathscr{R}, endowed with any norm; for instance, for any −∞<a<b<∞-\infty<a<b<\infty, one may consider the uniform norm ‖g‖a,b=supθ∈[a,b]n|g⁡(θ)|\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{a,b}=\sup_{\theta\in[a,b]^{n}}|g(\theta)| already used in (2.65).

Crucially, the hidden-model dynamics preserves the cone 𝒞\mathscr{C}: recalling that (et​ℒ)t≥0(e^{t\mathscr{L}})_{t\geq 0} denotes the hidden-model semigroup,

(3.4) et​ℒ​𝒞⊆𝒞​,t≥0​.e^{t\mathscr{L}}\mathscr{C}\subseteq\mathscr{C}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad t\geq 0\,\text{.}

Indeed, (2.43) gives et​ℒ​ℛ⊆ℛe^{t\mathscr{L}}\mathscr{R}\subseteq\mathscr{R}, while the Markov property of the hidden-model semigroup ensures that nonnegative functions remain nonnegative under the semigroup action.

We now record the first consequence of the positivity property in (3.4). The Perron–Frobenius theorem for an operator preserving a proper cone in a finite-dimensional space states that its spectral radius is an eigenvalue and admits a corresponding eigenfunction in the cone; see, e.g., [Van68, Theorem 3.1] and [SV70, Theorem 6]. In the present setting, the first assertion is in fact automatic: by (2.51), ℒ|ℛ\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{R}} is isospectral to a self-adjoint operator, and hence et​ℒ|ℛe^{t\mathscr{L}}|_{\mathscr{R}} has real positive spectrum. Hence, here the main role of the cone theorem is to locate an eigenfunction associated with its spectral radius inside 𝒞\mathscr{C}.

The same conclusion applies to the dual operator. More precisely, let ℛ′≔{h:ℛ→ℝ​linear}\mathscr{R}^{\prime}\coloneqq\{h:\mathscr{R}\to\mathbb{R}\ \text{linear}\} be the dual space of ℛ\mathscr{R}, and let

(3.5) 𝒞′≔{h∈ℛ′:h⁡(g)≥0​for every​g∈𝒞}\mathscr{C}^{\prime}\coloneqq\{h\in\mathscr{R}^{\prime}:h(g)\geq 0\ \text{for every}\ g\in\mathscr{C}\}

be the dual cone. If we endow ℛ\mathscr{R} with the norm ‖⋅‖a,b\left\lVert{\,\cdot\,}\right\rVert_{a,b} for some −∞<a<b<∞-\infty<a<b<\infty, then ℛ′\mathscr{R}^{\prime} carries the corresponding dual norm ‖h‖a,b≔sup‖g‖a,b=1|h⁡(g)|\left\lVert h\right\rVert_{a,b}\coloneqq\sup_{\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{a,b}=1}|h(g)|, h∈ℛ′h\in\mathscr{R}^{\prime}. Remark that, since 𝒞\mathscr{C} has nonempty interior, every nonzero element of 𝒞′\mathscr{C}^{\prime} is strictly positive on int⁡(𝒞){\rm int}(\mathscr{C}), that is,

(3.6) h⁡(g)>0​,0≠h∈𝒞′​,​g∈int⁡(𝒞)​.h(g)>0\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad 0\neq h\in\mathscr{C}^{\prime}\;\text{,}\;\;g\in{\rm int}(\mathscr{C})\,\text{.}

In what follows, for h∈ℛ′h\in\mathscr{R}^{\prime}, we write

(3.7) (h​ℒ)​(g)≔h⁡(ℒ​g)​,g∈ℛ​.(h\mathscr{L})(g)\coloneqq h(\mathscr{L}g)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad g\in\mathscr{R}\,\text{.}

Applying Perron–Frobenius theory to the hidden-model semigroup and its dual, and then using the spectral mapping theorem, yields the following.

Proposition 3.1 (Perron eigenfunctions I).

There exist 0≠g∗∈𝒞0\neq g_{\ast}\in\mathscr{C}, 0≠h∗∈𝒞′0\neq h_{\ast}\in\mathscr{C}^{\prime} satisfying

(3.8) ℒ​g∗=−gap2,∗​(α,w)​g∗andh∗​ℒ=−gap2,∗​(α,w)​h∗​.\mathscr{L}g_{\ast}=-{\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w)g_{\ast}\qquad\text{and}\qquad h_{\ast}\mathscr{L}=-{\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w)h_{\ast}\,\text{.}

We also refer to g∗g_{\ast} and h∗h_{\ast} as, respectively, right and left Perron eigenfunctions of ℒ|ℛ\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{R}}.

We stress that Proposition 3.1 requires no geometric assumption on the weights: it holds for arbitrary positive site weights α\alpha and nonnegative block weights ww.

For the comparison arguments developed in Section 5, the mere existence of Perron eigenfunctions will not suffice. In fact, we shall need both g∗g_{\ast} and h∗h_{\ast} to be:

  • •

    unique up to positive scaling;

  • •

    nondegenerate, in the sense that g∗∈int⁡(𝒞)g_{\ast}\in{\rm int}(\mathscr{C}) and h∗∈int⁡(𝒞′)h_{\ast}\in{\rm int}(\mathscr{C}^{\prime}).

Here, int⁡(𝒞){\rm int}(\mathscr{C}) is described in (3.3), whereas, as 𝒞⊆ℛ\mathscr{C}\subseteq\mathscr{R} is a finite-dimensional proper (i.e., closed, convex and pointed) cone,

(3.9) int⁡(𝒞′)={h∈𝒞′:h⁡(g)>0​for every​g∈𝒞∖{0}}​.{\rm int}(\mathscr{C}^{\prime})=\{h\in\mathscr{C}^{\prime}:h(g)>0\ \text{for every}\ g\in\mathscr{C}\setminus\{0\}\}\,\text{.}

These stronger conclusions rest on a corresponding strengthening of (3.4), that is, the strong positivity of the hidden-model semigroup, i.e.,

(3.10) et​ℒ​(𝒞∖{0})⊆int⁡(𝒞)​,t>0​.e^{t\mathscr{L}}(\mathscr{C}\setminus\{0\})\subseteq{\rm int}(\mathscr{C})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad t>0\,\text{.}

Unlike (3.4), strong positivity need not hold for arbitrary hypergraph weights. It does, however, hold under a natural geometric condition on the block weights, which will turn out to be optimal when analyzing spectral gaps.

3.2. Strong positivity

The aim of this section is to establish (3.10) under optimal geometric conditions. Since both the relevant condition and the proof of strong positivity take a particularly transparent form when ww induces a graph, we treat the graph and hypergraph cases separately when needed.

Graph case.

When ww induces a graph, connectivity alone upgrades the positivity property (3.4) to strong positivity.

Proposition 3.2 (Strong positivity: graph case).

Assume that n≥3n\geq 3, that ww satisfies (1.41), and that the graph induced by ww is connected. Then, the strong-positivity property (3.10) holds.

For the proof of this and the next result, see Section 3.3 below.

Hypergraph case.

For general block weights, connectivity alone is not sufficient for strong positivity, and the appropriate condition is expressed through the notion of a minimal hypergraph, which we now introduce.

Recall that a partition of [n][n] as in (1.46) is ww-compatible if every block BB with wB>0w_{B}>0 is either contained in one of its atoms or is a union of atoms, and that, under (1.35)–(1.36), its coarsest partition is the unique one with the smallest number of atoms. We call the hypergraph induced by ww minimal if ww satisfies (1.35)–(1.36) and its coarsest partition is the discrete partition [n]={1}⊔⋯⊔{n}[n]=\{1\}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\{n\}. Equivalently, a minimal hypergraph is connected, with w[n]=0w_{[n]}=0, and admits no nontrivial ww-compatible partition. On the other hand, connectedness plus w[n]=0w_{[n]}=0 is strictly weaker than minimality, as the example in Figure 3.1 shows.

Proposition 3.3 (Strong positivity: hypergraph case).

Assume that the hypergraph induced by ww is minimal as defined above. Then, the strong-positivity property (3.10) holds.

Remark 3.4.

In the graph case (1.41), minimality reduces to ordinary connectivity. Hence, under (1.41), Proposition 3.3 reduces to Proposition 3.2, as expected.

Before turning to the proof of Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, we record some important implications of the strong-positivity property (3.10).

Perron–Frobenius consequences.

The strong Perron–Frobenius theorem for an operator preserving a proper cone in a finite-dimensional space states that, if every nonzero element of the cone is mapped into its interior, then the spectral radius is an algebraically simple eigenvalue, strictly larger in modulus than every other eigenvalue, and its eigenfunction is unique up to positive scaling and belongs to the interior of the cone; see, e.g., [Van68, Theorem 4.4] or [SV70, Theorems 2 and 5]. The same conclusions hold for the dual operator. Indeed, strong positivity on 𝒞\mathscr{C} implies strong positivity on the dual cone 𝒞′\mathscr{C}^{\prime}: if 0≠h∈𝒞′0\neq h\in\mathscr{C}^{\prime} and 0≠g∈𝒞0\neq g\in\mathscr{C}, then

(3.11) h⁡(et​ℒ​g)>0​,t>0​.h(e^{t\mathscr{L}}g)>0\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad t>0\,\text{.}

Thus, the right and left Perron eigenfunctions lie in int⁡(𝒞){\rm int}(\mathscr{C}) and int⁡(𝒞′){\rm int}(\mathscr{C}^{\prime}), respectively; see (3.3) and (3.9). Applying these conclusions to et​ℒ|ℛe^{t\mathscr{L}}|_{\mathscr{R}} and using the spectral mapping theorem gives the following strengthening of Proposition 3.1.

Proposition 3.5 (Perron eigenfunctions II).

Under the assumptions of either Proposition 3.2 or Proposition 3.3, the eigenvalue −gap2,∗​(α,w)-{\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w) of ℒ|ℛ\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{R}} is algebraically simple. Moreover, the right and left Perron eigenfunctions g∗g_{\ast} and h∗h_{\ast} from Proposition 3.1 are unique up to multiplication by a positive scalar and satisfy

(3.12) g∗∈int⁡(𝒞)andh∗∈int⁡(𝒞′)​.g_{\ast}\in{\rm int}(\mathscr{C})\qquad\text{and}\qquad h_{\ast}\in{\rm int}(\mathscr{C}^{\prime})\,\text{.}
Remark 3.6.

The condition g∗∈int⁡(𝒞)g_{\ast}\in{\rm int}(\mathscr{C}) is precisely the nondegeneracy of the right Perron eigenfunction: g∗​(θ)>0g_{\ast}(\theta)>0 for every nonconstant θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Actually, more is true: after fixing a normalization of g∗g_{\ast}, there exist constants C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0, depending only on α\alpha and ww, such that

(3.13) C1​Varπ​(θ)≤g∗​(θ)≤C2​Varπ​(θ)​,θ∈ℝn​.C_{1}{\rm Var}_{\pi}(\theta)\leq g_{\ast}(\theta)\leq C_{2}{\rm Var}_{\pi}(\theta)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,\text{.}

In particular, g∗∈int⁡(𝒞)g_{\ast}\in{\rm int}(\mathscr{C}) provides a suitable substitute for Varπ{\rm Var}_{\pi} in (1.91). 3.3. Proof of strong positivity

The proofs of Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 rely on two ingredients. The first, Lemma 3.7, is a support argument requiring no geometric assumption on ww: zeros of a nonnegative quadratic function propagate along every finite sequence of hidden-model updates. The second, Lemma 3.8, is geometric: under the assumptions of either proposition, the linear range in (3.16) generated by such updates equals ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} whenever the initial configuration is nonconstant.

We start by introducing some notation. Recall from (1.70)–(1.71) and (2.2) that, for the (α,w)(\alpha,w)-KMP{\rm KMP} model, the support of its update measure equals

(3.15) supp(Υ)={KBU:B⊆[n]withwB>0,U∈[0,1]Band∑x∈BUx=1}.{\rm supp}(\Upsilon)=\big\{\textstyle K_{B}^{U}:B\subseteq[n]\ \text{with}\ w_{B}>0\,,\,U\in[0,1]^{B}\ \text{and}\ \sum_{x\in B}U_{x}=1\big\}\,\text{.}

Indeed, conditionally on the choice of BB, the redistribution vector has law Dir⁡(αB){\rm Dir}(\alpha^{B}), whose support is the whole probability simplex on BB. Further, for θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, define

(3.16) 𝒮(θ)=𝒮Υ(θ)≔span{Kℓ⋯K1θ:ℓ≥0,K1,…,Kℓ∈supp(Υ)}⊆ℝn\mathcal{S}(\theta)=\mathcal{S}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}(\theta)\coloneqq{\rm span}\big\{K_{\ell}\cdots K_{1}\theta:\ell\geq 0\,,\,K_{1},\ldots,K_{\ell}\in{\rm supp}(\Upsilon)\big\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}

as the linear range generated by applying finitely many successive updates from supp⁡(Υ){\rm supp}(\Upsilon) to θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Since the empty sequence of updates is allowed, one always has θ∈𝒮⁡(θ)\theta\in\mathcal{S}(\theta).

The next result is the first step in the proof of Propositions 3.2 and 3.3.

Let g∈𝒞g\in\mathscr{C}, θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and t>0t>0. If

Remark 3.10 (Even-degree cones).

Thus far, we have focused exclusively on the quadratic positive cone 𝒞⊆ℛ=ℛ2,∗\mathscr{C}\subseteq\mathscr{R}=\mathscr{R}_{2,\ast}. More generally, we could have considered, for every k≥1k\geq 1,

Thus, letting 𝒞k,∗′\mathscr{C}_{k,\ast}^{\prime} denote the dual cone, the Perron–Frobenius argument of Proposition 3.1 yields nonzero right and left Perron eigenfunctions gk,∗∈𝒞k,∗g_{k,\ast}\in\mathscr{C}_{k,\ast} and hk,∗∈𝒞k,∗′h_{k,\ast}\in\mathscr{C}_{k,\ast}^{\prime} such that

The strong-positivity and uniqueness conclusions of Proposition 3.5, however, seem specific to the quadratic cone and need not hold for k≥4k\geq 4: taking, e.g., k=4k=4 and the three-site segment, the hidden-model semigroup does not map the polynomial θ⟼g⁡(θ)=(θ1−θ2)2​(θ2−θ3)2∈𝒞4,∗∖{0}\theta\longmapsto g(\theta)=(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2})^{2}(\theta_{2}-\theta_{3})^{2}\in\mathscr{C}_{4,\ast}\setminus\{0\} into int⁡(𝒞4,∗){\rm int}(\mathscr{C}_{4,\ast}), as et​ℒ​g​(θ)=0e^{t\mathscr{L}}g(\theta)=0 for every t≥0t\geq 0 if either θ1=θ2\theta_{1}=\theta_{2} or θ2=θ3\theta_{2}=\theta_{3}.

4. Hypergraph reduction and gaps of KMP{\rm KMP}

Before turning to the comparison of gap1​(α,w){\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w) and gap2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w) (Section 5), we reduce the underlying weighted hypergraph to a minimal one; readers interested only in graphs, rather than general hypergraphs, may proceed directly to Section 5, as (1.35)–(1.36) and (1.41) alone already imply minimality.

Throughout, we fix positive site weights α\alpha and nonnegative block weights ww.

Recall that the hypergraph strong-positivity result of Proposition 3.3 requires minimality, whereas the assumptions of our main theorems from Section 1.2 impose only (1.35)–(1.36), namely, w[n]=0w_{[n]}=0 and connectedness. This apparent discrepancy is removed by collapsing the atoms of its coarsest partition into new sites. The main goal of this section is to prove that the resulting quotient hypergraph is minimal and, more importantly, preserves the relevant gaps: for each k≥1k\geq 1, gapk,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{k,\ast}(\alpha,w) coincides with the corresponding gap of the quotient KMP{\rm KMP} model with aggregated site weights. This is the content of Propositions 4.1–4.2 below. Thus, after this reduction, minimality may be assumed without loss of generality when proving the main results in Section 5.

We first need a few additional definitions. Recall from (1.46) that a partition

(4.1) [n]=N1⊔⋯⊔Nm​,2≤m≤n​,[n]=N_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup N_{m}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad 2\leq m\leq n\;\text{,}\;\;

is ww-compatible if every block BB with wB>0w_{B}>0 is either contained in one atom or is a union of them. Such a partition exists, since the discrete partition is ww-compatible. Fix one and, for j∈[m]j\in[m] and J⊆[m]J\subseteq[m], set

(4.2) NJ≔⨆j∈JNj​,α¯j≔α⁡(Nj)=∑x∈Njαx​,w¯J≔{wNJif​|J|≥2​,0if​|J|≤1​.N_{J}\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{j\in J}N_{j}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\bar{\alpha}_{j}\coloneqq\alpha(N_{j})=\textstyle\sum_{x\in N_{j}}\alpha_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\bar{w}_{J}\coloneqq\begin{cases}w_{N_{J}}&\text{if}\ |J|\geq 2\;\text{,}\\ 0&\text{if}\ |J|\leq 1\,\text{.}\end{cases}

We call the weighted hypergraph on [m][m] with site weights α¯=(α¯j)j∈[m]\bar{\alpha}=(\bar{\alpha}_{j})_{j\in[m]} and block weights w¯=(w¯J)J⊆[m]\bar{w}=(\bar{w}_{J})_{J\subseteq[m]} the quotient hypergraph associated with (4.1).

Proposition 4.1 (Minimal-hypergraph reduction).

Assume (1.35)–(1.36), and let (4.1) be its coarsest partition. Then the associated quotient hypergraph is minimal.

Proof.

Suppose that the quotient hypergraph were disconnected, and let C1,…,CℓC_{1},\ldots,C_{\ell}, ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, denote its connected components. Merging the original atoms according to these components gives the partition

(4.3) [n]=N1′⊔⋯⊔Nℓ′​,Na′≔⨆j∈CaNj​.[n]=N_{1}^{\prime}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup N_{\ell}^{\prime}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad N_{a}^{\prime}\coloneqq\bigsqcup_{j\in C_{a}}N_{j}\,\text{.}

This partition is again ww-compatible. Indeed, a block contained in some NjN_{j} remains internal. If instead a block is of the form NJN_{J} with w¯J=wNJ>0\bar{w}_{J}=w_{N_{J}}>0, then the quotient block JJ cannot meet two distinct connected components, and hence NJN_{J} is contained in one of the Na′N_{a}^{\prime}.

Since the original hypergraph is connected and m≥2m\geq 2, some block B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] with wB>0w_{B}>0 must meet at least two atoms. Thus, at least one component CaC_{a} contains at least two quotient sites, and consequently 2≤ℓ<m2\leq\ell<m. This contradicts the coarseness of the original partition (4.1). Hence, the quotient hypergraph is connected.

If m=2m=2, its only possible block connecting the two quotient sites is [2][2]. However, w¯[2]=w[n]=0\bar{w}_{[2]}=w_{[n]}=0 by (1.35), contradicting quotient connectivity. Therefore m≥3m\geq 3. Finally, if the quotient admitted a compatible partition

(4.4) [m]=C1⊔⋯⊔Cℓ​,1<ℓ<m​,[m]=C_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup C_{\ell}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad 1<\ell<m\;\text{,}\;\;

then replacing each CaC_{a} by ⊔j∈CaNj\sqcup_{j\in C_{a}}N_{j} would produce a ww-compatible partition of [n][n] with fewer than mm atoms. This is again impossible by coarseness. The quotient hypergraph is therefore minimal. ∎

Only in the next proposition, where KMP{\rm KMP} models with different numbers of sites are considered simultaneously, we indicate the number of sites by a superscript. Thus, for the original model on [n][n], we write, for instance, ℒ[n]=ℒ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle[n]}=\mathcal{L} and gapk,∗[n]​(α,w)=gapk,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle[n]}(\alpha,w)={\rm gap}_{k,\ast}(\alpha,w) for the objects defined in (1.6) and (1.28), respectively; the corresponding objects for the quotient model on [m][m] carry the superscript [m][m].

Proposition 4.2 (Hypergraph reduction and gaps).

Given a ww-compatible partition as in (4.1), one has, for the corresponding weights defined in (4.2),

(4.5) gapk,∗[n]​(α,w)=gapk,∗[m]​(α¯,w¯)​,k≥1​.{\rm gap}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle[n]}(\alpha,w)={\rm gap}_{k,\ast}^{\scriptscriptstyle[m]}(\bar{\alpha},\bar{w})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 1\,\text{.}
Proof.

5. One- and two-particle gaps of KMP{\rm KMP}

In this section, we compare gap1​(α,w){\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w) and gap2,∗​(α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\alpha,w), and prove the results stated in Section 1.2. The Perron–Frobenius theory developed in Section 3, together with the strong-positivity results of Section 3.2, is central to this comparison.

The section is organized in three main parts: we first establish strict monotonicity in the scale parameter τ\tau, and then analyze separately the limiting regimes τ→∞\tau\to\infty and τ→0\tau\to 0. These are the contents, respectively, of Sections 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3. At the end, we collect these ingredients and show how they yield Theorems 1.4, 1.5, 1.6 and 1.8 in Section 5.4.

Throughout this section, we fix positive site weights α\alpha and nonnegative block weights ww. For most of the analysis, in view of Propositions 4.1–4.2, we assume without loss of generality that ww induces a minimal hypergraph. Readers interested only in graphs (1.41) may simply assume that n≥3n\geq 3 and that ww induces a connected graph.

5.1. Two-particle gap monotonicity

The main goal of this section is to prove that the map in (1.37) is strictly increasing anytime the underlying hypergraph is minimal.

Proposition 5.1 (Monotonicity).

For all positive site weights α\alpha and nonnegative block weights ww inducing a minimal hypergraph, the map (0,∞)∋τ⟼gap2,∗​(τ​α,w)∈(0,∞)(0,\infty)\ni\tau\longmapsto{\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\tau\alpha,w)\in(0,\infty) is continuous and strictly increasing.

Remark 5.4.

Proposition 5.1 shows that hypergraph minimality—or, in view of Propositions 4.1–4.2, conditions (1.35)–(1.36)—ensures the strict monotonicity of τ↦λτ\tau\mapsto\lambda_{\tau}. Without these geometric assumptions, strict monotonicity may fail (take, e.g., wB=𝟙|B|=nw_{B}=\mathds{1}_{|B|=n}, in which case gapk,∗​(α,w)=1{\rm gap}_{k,\ast}(\alpha,w)=1 for every k≥1k\geq 1 and α\alpha), although the map remains nondecreasing. Since this weaker statement will not be needed, we leave its verification to the reader.

Remark 5.5 (Directional vs. componentwise monotonicity).

The monotonicity in Proposition 5.1 is directional: it holds along the rays τ⟼τ​α\tau\longmapsto\tau\alpha, but not under arbitrary componentwise increases of the site weights. Indeed, let n=3n=3 and wB=𝟙|B|=2w_{B}=\mathds{1}_{|B|=2}. For α=(1,1,1)\alpha=(1,1,1) and α′=(s,s,1)\alpha^{\prime}=(s,s,1), s≥1s\geq 1, one has α≤α′\alpha\leq\alpha^{\prime} componentwise, whereas

Proposition 5.1 and Remark 5.2 establish Theorem 1.5 for minimal hypergraphs, while Propositions 4.1–4.2 lifts this result to the original setting of Theorem 1.5, thereby recovering the statement in its full form. Consequently, there exists a unique threshold τc​(α,w)∈[0,∞]\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)\in[0,\infty] separating the regime in which gap2,∗​(τ​α,w){\rm gap}_{2,\ast}(\tau\alpha,w) is smaller than gap1​(τ​α,w){\rm gap}_{1}(\tau\alpha,w) from that in which the reverse inequality holds. To characterize the extremal cases τc​(α,w)∈{0,∞}\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)\in\{0,\infty\}, in Sections 5.2 and 5.3 we analyze the gaps of the limiting dynamics obtained as τ→∞\tau\to\infty and τ→0\tau\to 0, respectively. We begin with the former.

5.2. The limit τ→∞\tau\to\infty

To study the extremal regime τ→∞\tau\to\infty, it is convenient to work directly with the limiting hidden-model dynamics. Indeed, for every nonempty block B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n],

(5.16) Dir⁡(τ​αB)⟹δπBas​τ→∞​,{\rm Dir}(\tau\alpha^{B})\Longrightarrow\delta_{\pi_{B}}\qquad\text{as}\ \tau\to\infty\;\text{,}\;\;

where πB\pi_{B} is the BB-conditional measure on [n][n] given in (5.3). Thus, each random Dirichlet redistribution degenerates into the deterministic weighted averaging of the coordinates in BB. This defines a Markov dynamics also at τ=∞\tau=\infty, namely, the hidden model associated with a block variant of the averaging process. The latter process, originally introduced by Aldous, has received considerable attention in recent years; see, e.g., [AL12, QS23].

We first introduce this limiting hidden dynamics and relate its generator to ℒτ\mathscr{L}_{\tau} by operator-norm convergence. We then compute its action on the spatial variance, obtaining the limiting lower bound λ∞≥gap1​(α,w)\lambda_{\infty}\geq{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w), together with the quantitative finite-τ\tau estimate from Theorem 1.4. Finally, we characterize the geometries for which equality holds and establish the strict upper bound λ∞<2​gap1​(α,w)\lambda_{\infty}<2{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w), including the sharpness of the constant 22.

5.2.1. The limiting hidden model

Recall that πx=αx/α0\pi_{x}=\alpha_{x}/\alpha_{0} and π⁡(B)=α⁡(B)/α0\pi(B)=\alpha(B)/\alpha_{0}. 5.3. The limit τ→0\tau\to 0

We now turn to the regime τ→0\tau\to 0, with the goal of proving the first inequality in (1.38) and characterizing the geometries for which τc​(α,w)=0\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0.

As τ→0\tau\to 0, the Dirichlet redistribution law concentrates on the vertices of the simplex: for every nonempty B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] with wB>0w_{B}>0,

(5.53) Dir⁡(τ​αB)⟹∑z∈Bπz|B​eezas ​τ→0​,{\rm Dir}(\tau\alpha^{B})\Longrightarrow\sum_{z\in B}\pi_{z|B}\,e_{e_{z}}\qquad\text{as }\tau\to 0\;\text{,}\;\;

where πz|B\pi_{z|B} is defined in (5.3) and (ez)z∈B(e_{z})_{z\in B} are the vertices of the simplex on BB. Consequently, in the limiting hidden-model dynamics, when the clock of BB rings, a site Z∈BZ\in B is sampled with law πB\pi_{B}, all coordinates in BB are replaced by the common value θZ\theta_{Z}, and the coordinates outside BB are left unchanged.

The corresponding particle dynamics admits an equally simple description: all particles lying in the updated block are sent to the same sampled site ZZ. Thus, once two particles meet, they subsequently move together as a single particle, effectively reducing the system to one with fewer particles. When one restricts attention to a fixed particle number, such mergers are instead recorded as killing: the process is stopped as soon as two particles coalesce.

We shall use both viewpoints. The hidden-model description gives a direct passage from the finite-τ\tau setup to the limiting dynamics, whereas the particle-system description, through a direct intertwining at τ=0\tau=0, identifies the limiting eigenvalue with the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue of a killed two-particle chain.

5.3.1. The limiting hidden model

We now introduce the candidate limiting hidden-model dynamics obtained by letting τ→0\tau\to 0 in the generators ℒτ\mathscr{L}_{\tau}, and make this convergence precise in Lemma 5.14 below.

For every g∈ℛ=ℛ2,∗g\in\mathscr{R}=\mathscr{R}_{2,\ast}, define

(5.59) ΠB,2†​ψ​(x,y)≔{ψ⁡(x,y)if​x,y∉BΠB,1​ψ​(⋅,y)​(x)=∑z∈Bπz|B​ψ​(z,y)if​x∈B,y∉BΠB,1​ψ​(x,⋅)​(y)=∑z∈Bπz|B​ψ​(x,z)if​x∉B,y∈B0if​x,y∈B​.\Pi_{B,2}^{\dagger}\psi(x,y)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\textstyle\psi(x,y)&\text{if}\ x,y\notin B\\ \textstyle\Pi_{B,1}\psi({\,\cdot\,},y)(x)=\sum_{z\in B}\pi_{z|B}\,\psi(z,y)&\text{if}\ x\in B,y\notin B\\ \textstyle\Pi_{B,1}\psi(x,{\,\cdot\,})(y)=\sum_{z\in B}\pi_{z|B}\,\psi(x,z)&\text{if}\ x\notin B,y\in B\\ 0&\text{if}\ x,y\in B\,\text{.}\end{cases}

(5.60) L2†≔∑B⊆[n]wB​(ΠB,2†−I)​.L_{2}^{\dagger}\coloneqq\sum_{B\subseteq[n]}w_{B}\,\big(\Pi_{B,2}^{\dagger}-I\big)\,\text{.}

Before killing, each particle marginally follows the one-particle dynamics, with each block BB ringing at rate wBw_{B} and relocating any particle it contains according to πB\pi_{B}, until the first update involving both particles, at which time they merge and the two-particle process is killed.

Remark 5.15.

Even when ww induces a connected hypergraph, this killed dynamics need not be irreducible on [n]≠2[n]^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\neq}; the form and number of its communicating classes depend on the underlying geometry and will play a central role in Proposition 5.18 below.

Indeed, transposition (x,y)↦(y,x)(x,y)\mapsto(y,x) commutes with L2†L_{2}^{\dagger}. Consider a communicating class attaining the smallest principal Dirichlet eigenvalue. If the class is invariant under transposition, uniqueness of its positive principal eigenfunction makes this eigenfunction symmetric. Otherwise, the class and its transpose are distinct, and the sum of their positive principal eigenfunctions is now a symmetric eigenfunction. Thus, the smallest Dirichlet eigenvalue is always attained in ℋ≠\mathscr{H}_{\scriptscriptstyle\neq}.

This observation will be crucial below; see, e.g., (5.75). Indeed, we shall mainly consider antisymmetric L2†L_{2}^{\dagger}-eigenfunctions of the form

We may now complete the limiting comparison announced in Section 1.2.

5.3.3. Geometries corresponding to τc​(α,w)=0\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0

The preceding section identifies λ0\lambda_{0} with the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue of the killed two-particle system. We now characterize equality in (5.71), which, by strict monotonicity, is precisely the regime τc​(α,w)=0\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0.

Proposition 5.18 (Characterization of τc​(α,w)=0\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0).

Assume that ww induces a minimal hypergraph. Then, for every positive α\alpha, the following are equivalent:

    after a relabeling of [n][n], every B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] with wB>0w_{B}>0 and |B|≥2|B|\geq 2 is an interval.

(5.76) λ0=gap1​(α,w)​<λτ​,τ>​0​.\lambda_{0}={\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)<\lambda_{\tau}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\tau>0\,\text{.}

(5.77) τc(α,w)=0⟺λ0=gap1(α,w).\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda_{0}={\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)\,\text{.}

(5.78) Nj≔{x∈[n]:ϕ⁡(x)=aj}​,j=1,…,m​.N_{j}\coloneqq\big\{x\in[n]:\phi(x)=a_{j}\big\}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad j=1,\ldots,m\,\text{.}

Since ϕ\phi is nonconstant, m≥2m\geq 2. By the intertwining used in the proof of Proposition 5.17,

(5.79) L2†​𝒟​ϕ=−gap1​(α,w)​𝒟​ϕ=−λ0​𝒟​ϕ​.L_{2}^{\dagger}\mathcal{D}\phi=-{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)\mathcal{D}\phi=-\lambda_{0}\mathcal{D}\phi\,\text{.}

Therefore, by the Perron–Frobenius discussion following (5.69), the restriction of 𝒟​ϕ\mathcal{D}\phi to each communicating class of the killed chain is either identically zero or has a strict sign.

Fix B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] with wB>0w_{B}>0. Suppose first that BB meets NiN_{i} and NkN_{k}, with i<ki<k, but misses some NjN_{j}, i<j<ki<j<k. Choose

(5.80) x∈B∩Ni​,y∈Nj∖B​,z∈B∩Nk​.x\in B\cap N_{i}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad y\in N_{j}\setminus B\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad z\in B\cap N_{k}\,\text{.}

The states (x,y)(x,y) and (z,y)(z,y) communicate through BB-updates of the L2†L_{2}^{\dagger}-dynamics, whereas

(5.81) 𝒟​ϕ​(x,y)=ai−aj<0​,𝒟​ϕ​(z,y)=ak−aj>0​,\mathcal{D}\phi(x,y)=a_{i}-a_{j}<0\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathcal{D}\phi(z,y)=a_{k}-a_{j}>0\;\text{,}\;\;

contradicting the preceding sign property. Hence, the level sets met by BB have consecutive indices.

Suppose next that BB meets at least two level sets but does not contain one of them. Then, for some i≠ji\neq j, we may choose

(5.82) x∈B∩Ni​,y∈Ni∖B​,z∈B∩Nj​.x\in B\cap N_{i}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad y\in N_{i}\setminus B\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad z\in B\cap N_{j}\,\text{.}

Again, (x,y)(x,y) and (z,y)(z,y) communicate, but

(5.83) 𝒟​ϕ​(x,y)=0​,𝒟​ϕ​(z,y)=aj−ai≠0​,\mathcal{D}\phi(x,y)=0\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathcal{D}\phi(z,y)=a_{j}-a_{i}\neq 0\;\text{,}\;\;

which is impossible on a communicating class on which 𝒟​ϕ\mathcal{D}\phi is either identically zero or strictly signed. Thus, every positive-weight block is either contained in one level set or is a union of consecutive complete level sets. The partition

(5.84) [n]=N1⊔⋯⊔Nm[n]=N_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup N_{m}

is therefore ww-compatible. Minimality and m≥2m\geq 2 force m=nm=n, so every NjN_{j} is a singleton. Relabeling the sites according to the increasing values of ϕ\phi proves the interval condition.

Conversely, assume that the sites are labeled so that every positive-weight block of size at least two is an interval. Since every ΠB,1\Pi_{B,1} preserves nondecreasing functions, the one-particle semigroup is monotone. Hence, by [LP17, Lemma 22.17], there exists a nonconstant nondecreasing eigenfunction ϕ\phi such that

(5.85) L1​ϕ=−gap1​(α,w)​ϕ​.L_{1}\phi=-{\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)\phi\,\text{.}

We claim that ϕ\phi is strictly increasing.

Suppose that ϕ⁡(i)=ϕ⁡(i+1)\phi(i)=\phi(i+1) for some i=1,…,n−1i=1,\ldots,n-1. Taking the difference of (5.85) at i+1i+1 and ii gives

(5.86) 0=L1​ϕ​(i+1)−L1​ϕ​(i)=∑B∋i+1B∌iwB​(πB​(ϕ)−ϕ⁡(i+1))+∑B∋iB∌i+1wB​(ϕ⁡(i)−πB​(ϕ))​.0=L_{1}\phi(i+1)-L_{1}\phi(i)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}B\ni i+1\\ B\not\ni i\end{subarray}}w_{B}\bigl(\pi_{B}(\phi)-\phi(i+1)\bigr)+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}B\ni i\\ B\not\ni i+1\end{subarray}}w_{B}\bigl(\phi(i)-\pi_{B}(\phi)\bigr)\,\text{.}

Every term on the right-hand side is nonnegative. Indeed, an interval containing i+1i+1 but not ii lies to the right of ii, while an interval containing ii but not i+1i+1 lies to its left. Consequently, equality in (5.86) implies that ϕ\phi is constant on every positive-weight block starting at i+1i+1 or ending at ii. Let [n]=N1⊔⋯⊔Nm[n]=N_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup N_{m} be the partition into the level sets of ϕ\phi, ordered according to their values. Since ϕ\phi is nondecreasing, the sets NjN_{j} are intervals. We claim that every positive-weight block BB is either contained in one NjN_{j}, or is a union of consecutive level sets. Indeed, suppose that BB meets more than one level set and starts strictly inside some NjN_{j}. If a=min⁡Ba=\min B, then ϕ⁡(a−1)=ϕ⁡(a)\phi(a-1)=\phi(a), while BB starts at aa and contains points where ϕ>ϕ⁡(a)\phi>\phi(a). This contradicts the conclusion drawn from (5.86). The analogous argument at max⁡B\max B shows that BB cannot end strictly inside a level set. The claim follows.

Thus, the partition (N1,…,Nm)(N_{1},\ldots,N_{m}) is ww-compatible. Since ϕ\phi is nonconstant, m≥2m\geq 2, while minimality excludes 2≤m<n2\leq m<n. Therefore m=nm=n, and

(5.87) ϕ⁡(1)<ϕ⁡(2)<⋯<ϕ⁡(n)​.\phi(1)<\phi(2)<\cdots<\phi(n)\,\text{.}

Before killing, the two-particle dynamics cannot change the order of the two coordinates: if an interval BB contains exactly one coordinate of (x,y)(x,y), relocating that coordinate inside BB cannot move it across the other one. Hence, every communicating class is contained in one of the two sets

(5.88) {(x,y)∈[n]≠2:x<y}or{(x,y)∈[n]≠2:x>y}​.\big\{(x,y)\in[n]^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\neq}:x<y\big\}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\big\{(x,y)\in[n]^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\neq}:x>y\big\}\,\text{.}

By (5.87), 𝒟​ϕ\mathcal{D}\phi has a strict sign on every communicating class. Since it is a gap1​(α,w){\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)-eigenfunction of −L2†-L_{2}^{\dagger}, Perron–Frobenius theory shows that gap1​(α,w){\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w) is the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue on every class. Recalling (5.68)–(5.69), we obtain

(5.89) λ0=gap1​(α,w)​.\lambda_{0}={\rm gap}_{1}(\alpha,w)\,\text{.}

The equivalence (5.77) and strict monotonicity then give (5.76). ∎

5.4. Proof of Theorems 1.4, 1.5, 1.6 and 1.8

We collect the results established above.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

The lower bound was proved in Corollary 5.8, while the upper bound and its extension to general hypergraphs were established in Proposition 5.11 and Remark 5.12. Sharpness of the two constants was proved in Remarks 5.9 and 5.13. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

For minimal hypergraphs, the claim follows from Proposition 5.1 and Remark 5.2. The general case follows from Propositions 4.1–4.2. ∎

Proof of Theorems 1.6 and 1.8.

For minimal hypergraphs, the characterizations of τc​(α,w)=∞\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=\infty and τc​(α,w)=0\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0 were established in Propositions 5.10 and 5.18, respectively.

We now remove the minimality assumption, retaining only (1.35)–(1.36). By Proposition 4.2, passing to any ww-compatible partition preserves gap1{\rm gap}_{1} and gap2,∗{\rm gap}_{2,\ast} at every scale τ>0\tau>0, and hence also λ0\lambda_{0}, λ∞\lambda_{\infty}, and τc\tau_{c}. Moreover, the quotient hypergraph associated with the coarsest partition is minimal (Proposition 4.1). Applying Proposition 5.18 to this quotient shows that τc​(α,w)=0\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=0 if and only if, after ordering the quotient sites, every positive-weight quotient block is an interval. This is precisely the segment-like condition in Theorem 1.81. Likewise, Proposition 5.10 yields the corresponding characterization of τc​(α,w)=∞\tau_{c}(\alpha,w)=\infty. This proves Theorem 1.8.

Theorem 1.6 then follows from the observation following the statement of its hypergraph counterpart. ∎

6. Boundary-driven KMP{\rm KMP}

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.11. The argument is based on a suitable decomposition of polynomials and on a killed-particle representation of their highest-degree components. In particular, it does not use the hidden model associated with the boundary-driven dynamics. That representation has instead played a central role in the description of the corresponding nonequilibrium steady state [DMFG24, GRT25].

6.1. Polynomials and killed particles

Recall from (2.1) and (1.20) that ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} denotes the space of functions ψ:[n]k→ℝ\psi:[n]^{k}\to\mathbb{R}, endowed with the L2​(μk)L^{2}(\mu_{k}) scalar product, whereas ℋk⊆ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k}\subseteq\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} is the subspace of symmetric functions. The generator LkL_{k} acts on ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} and describes the labeled kk-particle dynamics, while Lksym=Lk|ℋkL_{k}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}}=L_{k}|_{\mathscr{H}_{k}} describes its unlabeled counterpart. The same hat notation as in (2.13) will be used for polynomials on Ωbd\Omega_{\rm bd}: for ψ∈ℋk\psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k},

(6.1) ψ^(η)≔∑x1,…,xk∈[n]ψ(x1,…,xk)ηx1⋯ηxk,η∈Ωbd.\textstyle\widehat{\psi}(\eta)\coloneqq\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in[n]}\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\eta_{x_{1}}\cdots\eta_{x_{k}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\eta\in\Omega_{\rm bd}\,\text{.}

Since Ωbd\Omega_{\rm bd} has nonempty interior, the map in (6.1) is a linear isomorphism between ℋk\mathscr{H}_{k} and the homogeneous polynomials of degree kk on Ωbd\Omega_{\rm bd}.

Recall from Section 1.3.2 that 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k} denotes the space of polynomials of degree at most kk on Ωbd\Omega_{\rm bd}, with 𝒬−1≔0\mathscr{Q}_{-1}\coloneqq{0}. The generator ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} preserves each 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k}, but its action is no longer homogeneous: a reservoir update produces terms of degree strictly smaller than the original one. In Proposition 6.1 below we identify the action of ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} on the highest-degree component of a polynomial.

First, we introduce some notation. Recall (1.62)–(1.63) and (2.39), and define, for k≥1k\geq 1, the multiplication operator L∂,kL_{\partial,k} on ℋk⊗\mathscr{H}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes} by

(6.2) L∂,kψ(x1,…,xk)≔−ψ(x1,…,xk)∑x∈[n]ωx(1−𝐄x[Ux𝔫x​(x1,…,xk)]),\textstyle L_{\partial,k}\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\coloneqq-\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\sum_{x\in[n]}\omega_{x}\,(1-\mathbf{E}_{x}\big[U_{x}^{\mathfrak{n}_{x}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})}\big])\;\text{,}\;\;

for x1,…,xk∈[n]x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in[n]. Here, ωx\omega_{x}, UxU_{x} and 𝐄x\mathbf{E}_{x} are as in (1.61)–(1.62): 𝐄x\mathbf{E}_{x} denotes expectation with respect to the reservoir variables (Ux,ξx)(U_{x},\xi_{x}) associated with an update at xx, while ωx≥0\omega_{x}\geq 0 denotes the rate of such updates. The corresponding boundary-driven particle generator is

(6.3) Lbd,k≔Lk+L∂,k​,Lbd,ksym≔Lbd,k|ℋk​.L_{{\rm bd},k}\coloneqq L_{k}+L_{\partial,k}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad L_{{\rm bd},k}^{{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle sym}}}\coloneqq L_{{\rm bd},k}|_{\mathscr{H}_{k}}\,\text{.}

Since LkL_{k} is self-adjoint on L2​(μk)=L2​([n]k,μk)L^{2}(\mu_{k})=L^{2}([n]^{k},\mu_{k}) and L∂,kL_{\partial,k} is a nonpositive multiplication operator, Lbd,kL_{{\rm bd},k} is self-adjoint and sub-Markovian. Moreover, it commutes with permutations of the labels, so that ℋk\mathscr{H}_{k} is invariant.

The operator in (6.2) has the following probabilistic interpretation. At a reservoir update at xx, conditionally on UxU_{x}, each particle at xx survives independently with probability UxU_{x}; the process is killed as soon as at least one particle does not survive. Thus, 𝐄x​[Ux𝔫x]\mathbf{E}_{x}[U_{x}^{\mathfrak{n}_{x}}] is precisely the probability that all particles currently at xx survive the update.

Proposition 6.1 (Top-degree intertwining).

For every k≥1k\geq 1 and every ψ∈ℋk\psi\in\mathscr{H}_{k},

Remark 6.3 (The reversible case).

The above characterization of the polynomial spectrum of ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd} is valid in the general, not necessarily reversible, case. In the special case in which ρx≡ρ∗\rho_{x}\equiv\rho_{\ast} on supp⁡(ω){\rm supp}(\omega), the product Gamma measure in (1.64) is reversible. Then, self-adjointness and (1.65) imply that the orthogonal complement of 𝒬k−1\mathscr{Q}_{k-1} in 𝒬k\mathscr{Q}_{k} is invariant under ℒbd\mathcal{L}_{\rm bd}. Since polynomials are dense in L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu), the generator admits a complete orthonormal family of polynomial eigenfunctions, and its L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu)-spectrum coincides with the closure of the polynomial spectrum in (6.8). In particular, the polynomial gap in (1.67) is the usual L2​(ν)L^{2}(\nu)-spectral gap.

Remark 6.5 (Further reservoir mechanisms).

The family in (1.61) interpolates between several reservoir mechanisms considered in the literature. The choice

(6.18) βx=αx\beta_{x}=\alpha_{x}

corresponds to the boundary update used, for instance, in [DMFG24, GRT25]. For finite βx\beta_{x}, the factor UxU_{x} retains part of the energy present at xx before the update. At the opposite extreme,

(6.19) Ux​(ηx+ξx)⟹ξx′∼Gamma⁡(αx,ρx)​,as​βx→∞​,U_{x}(\eta_{x}+\xi_{x})\ \Longrightarrow\ \xi_{x}^{\prime}\sim{\rm Gamma}(\alpha_{x},\rho_{x})\;\text{,}\;\;\quad\text{as}\ \beta_{x}\to\infty\;\text{,}\;\;

with ξx′\xi_{x}^{\prime} being independent of ηx\eta_{x}, and one recovers the full-refresh mechanism [KMP82]; see also [CGGR13]. In particular, the original KMP reservoirs correspond, up to the choice of the boundary rates and temperatures, to αx=1\alpha_{x}=1 and βx=∞\beta_{x}=\infty: at each boundary update, the energy is replaced by an exponential random variable with mean ρx\rho_{x}. Conversely, as βx→0\beta_{x}\to 0, one has Ux→1U_{x}\to 1 and ξx→0\xi_{x}\to 0 in probability, so that the reservoir action becomes void. One may also allow ρx=0\rho_{x}=0, interpreting ξx=0\xi_{x}=0 almost surely, in which case the update only removes energy through the multiplication ηx⟼Ux​ηx\eta_{x}\longmapsto U_{x}\eta_{x}.

More generally, our proof does not rely on the beta–gamma form of the variables in (1.61). It only uses that, at an update of the reservoir attached to xx, the energy is replaced by

(6.20) ηx⟼Ux​(ηx+ξx)​,\eta_{x}\longmapsto U_{x}(\eta_{x}+\xi_{x})\;\text{,}\;\;

where (Ux,ξx)∈[0,1]×[0,∞)(U_{x},\xi_{x})\in[0,1]\times[0,\infty) is sampled independently of the current configuration and has finite moments of every order. The variables UxU_{x} and ξx\xi_{x} need not be independent. The same top-degree computation gives (6.2), and the killing-time argument is unchanged. The full-refresh update is covered directly by setting the coefficient of every positive-degree term equal to zero. Analogous block-reservoir mechanisms may be treated in the same way, at the cost of heavier notation.

7. Stochastic exchange models

The main goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.12 from Section 1.3.3. We begin by giving a rigorous construction of stochastic exchange models together with their associated hidden dynamics. The core of the proof of Theorem 1.12 occupies Sections 7.2–7.3, whereas examples of stochastic exchange models are discussed in Section 7.4.

7.1. Construction and first properties

Fix n≥2n\geq 2. Throughout, let

(7.1) 𝔐≔{M=(Mx​y)x,y∈[n]∈[0,1]n×n:M​𝟏=𝟏}⊆ℝn×n\mathfrak{M}\coloneqq\{M=(M_{xy})_{x,y\in[n]}\in[0,1]^{n\times n}:M\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}

Recall from Section 1.3.3 that the stochastic exchange model associated with Υ\Upsilon is built from the updates, with infinitesimal rate Υ⁡(d​M)\Upsilon({\rm d}M),

(7.3) η⟼η​M​,θ⟼M​θ​,\eta\longmapsto\eta M\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\theta\longmapsto M\theta\;\text{,}\;\;

where the first update acts on energy configurations η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega, regarded as row vectors, while the second defines the corresponding hidden dynamics on column vectors θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Row-stochasticity ensures that η​M∈Ω\eta M\in\Omega whenever η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega, as well as

(7.4) M​[a,b]n⊆[a,b]n​,−∞<a<b<∞​,M[a,b]^{n}\subseteq[a,b]^{n}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad-\infty<a<b<\infty\;\text{,}\;\;

since every coordinate of M​θM\theta is a convex combination of the coordinates of θ\theta. In particular, although the hidden dynamics is not conservative in general, every cube [a,b]n[a,b]^{n} is invariant and every flat configuration is fixed.

In the following proposition, we rigorously construct the stochastic exchange model and its hidden model starting from their infinitesimal descriptions. We show that the sole integrability condition (7.2) is sufficient both to make the corresponding generators well defined on the corresponding polynomial spaces and, through standard Hille–Yosida theory, to construct the associated Feller processes; see, e.g., [Lig05]. In particular, this construction allows Υ⁡(𝔐)\Upsilon(\mathfrak{M}) to be infinite. If instead Υ⁡(𝔐)<∞\Upsilon(\mathfrak{M})<\infty, as happens, for instance, for the KMP model, the conclusion is immediate, since the operators in (7.6) and (7.7) below extend uniquely to bounded Markov generators on the corresponding spaces of continuous functions.

Remark 7.2 (Invariant measures).

Both Ω\Omega and [a,b]n[a,b]^{n} are compact. Hence, by the Feller property and, e.g., [Lig05, Proposition I.1.8(f)], both processes admit invariant probability measures. Henceforth, μΥ\mu^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} denotes an arbitrary invariant probability measure of the stochastic exchange model on Ω\Omega.

Under the sole assumption (7.2), μΥ\mu^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} need not be unique. For instance, if Υ\Upsilon is supported on permutation matrices, the dynamics only permutes the coordinates of configurations η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega, and many invariant probability measures coexist. Proposition 7.6 below provides several equivalent characterizations of uniqueness, all involving only the second-order moments of the entries of M∈𝔐M\in\mathfrak{M} with respect to Υ\Upsilon.

In contrast, for the hidden process, invariant probability measures are never unique: row-stochasticity gives M⁡(c​𝟏)=c​𝟏M(c\mathbf{1})=c\mathbf{1} for every M∈𝔐M\in\mathfrak{M} and c∈[a,b]c\in[a,b], thus, δc​𝟏\delta_{c\mathbf{1}} is invariant.

7.2. Particle systems, polynomials, and intertwinings

This section develops, for general stochastic exchange models, the polynomial characterizations of the eigenvalue problem established for the KMP{\rm KMP} model in Section 2.1. This amounts to introducing the natural labeled-particle dynamics, identifying the corresponding linearly isomorphic polynomial spaces, and establishing the associated intertwining relations. Most of the objects introduced in Section 2.1 have natural analogues in the present setting, and the corresponding statements carry over verbatim. The main difference is that the particle system need not possess a canonical strictly positive reversible measure, which was used there to define the tilde maps (2.12)–(2.13) and characterize the spaces ℋk,∗\mathscr{H}_{k,\ast} and 𝒫k,∗\mathscr{P}_{k,\ast} (Proposition 2.5). For the algebraic study of the eigenvalue problem, it suffices to replace that measure, at each level kk, by an arbitrary strictly positive symmetric probability measure on [n]k[n]^{k}, say ϖk\varpi_{k}. Since ϖk\varpi_{k} need be neither invariant nor reversible for the particle dynamics, the corresponding statements require minor modifications, which we record below and summarize in Proposition 7.3. In this section, we retain most of the notation (e.g., ℋk,𝒫k,ℛk\mathscr{H}_{k},\mathscr{P}_{k},\mathscr{R}_{k}, and their tensor analogues) introduced in Section 2.1.

7.3. Proof of Theorem 1.12

In view of Proposition 7.3 and, in particular, (7.28)–(7.29), gap⁡(ℒΥ){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}) in (1.74) is determined by its hidden-model counterpart, namely, infk≥1gap⁡(ℒΥ|ℛk,∗)\inf_{k\geq 1}{\rm gap}(\mathscr{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}|_{\mathscr{R}_{k,\ast}}). The analysis of the latter lies at the core of the proof of the spectral-gap identities in Theorems 1.1–1.2. To prove the identity in (1.75), the core of the argument from Section 2.2 carries over essentially unchanged in this more general setting, after allowing for possibly complex eigenvalues and eigenfunctions.

Remark 7.4.

The ordering in (7.36), together with the isospectrality in (7.26), yields the ℒΥ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}-analogue of the KMP{\rm KMP} inequalities (2.69) from Remark 2.10.

Remark 7.5.

As observed in Remark 3.10, if k≥2k\geq 2 is even, the cone 𝒞k,∗\mathscr{C}_{k,\ast} of nonnegative functions in ℛk,∗\mathscr{R}_{k,\ast} is proper, has nonempty interior, and is preserved by the hidden-model semigroup. Assume that the Borel measure Υ\Upsilon on 𝔐\mathfrak{M} satisfies (7.2). Then, the following statements are equivalent:

Proof of Proposition 7.6.

We first prove the equivalence of 2 and 3. By (7.30) and (7.31),

(7.48) gap⁡(ℒΥ)=gap⁡(L2Υ|ℋ2)=gap⁡(L2Υ)​.{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon})={\rm gap}(L_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}|_{\mathscr{H}_{2}})={\rm gap}(L_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon})\,\text{.}

Recall that, for a finite-state Markov generator, zero is always an eigenvalue of the corresponding generator, and its multiplicity equals the number of closed communicating classes, while all the remaining eigenvalues of the generator have strictly negative real part. Hence, L2ΥL_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} admits a unique invariant probability measure if and only if gap⁡(L2Υ)>0{\rm gap}(L_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon})>0. 7.4. Examples

As already mentioned, the KMP{\rm KMP} model with site and block weights α\alpha and ww corresponds to the stochastic exchange model with the update measure Υ=ΥKMP\Upsilon=\Upsilon^{\rm\scriptscriptstyle KMP} in (1.70). We next discuss three further classes of stochastic exchange models: averaging-like processes, immediate exchange models, and the harmonic process. Some of these models with all update blocks of size two were recently studied in [KQS25, CKMP25]. Throughout this section, we fix n≥2n\geq 2.

7.4.1. Averaging processes and generalized exchanges

Fix a probability vector π=(πx)x∈[n]\pi=(\pi_{x})_{x\in[n]} with πx>0\pi_{x}>0 for every xx, and nonnegative block weights w=(wB)B⊆[n]w=(w_{B})_{B\subseteq[n]}. Recall from (2.2) that KBπK_{B}^{\pi} is the row-stochastic matrix which redistributes the total mass in BB deterministically according to the conditional probability vector (πx/π⁡(B))x∈B(\pi_{x}/\pi(B))_{x\in B} and leaves all coordinates outside BB unchanged. The corresponding block averaging process is obtained from

(7.58) Υ=ΥAVG≔∑B⊆[n]wB​δKBπ​.\textstyle\Upsilon=\Upsilon^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle AVG}}\coloneqq\sum_{B\subseteq[n]}w_{B}\,\delta_{K_{B}^{\pi}}\,\text{.}

This is precisely the update measure underlying the limiting hidden generator ℒ∞\mathscr{L}_{\infty} in (5.17); its support is the set supp⁡(Υ∞){\rm supp}(\Upsilon_{\infty}) introduced in (3.31). For pairwise blocks, the update on the coordinates {x,y}\{x,y\} reads

(7.59) (ηx,ηy)​(πxπx+πyπyπx+πyπxπx+πyπyπx+πy)=(πxπx+πy​(ηx+ηy),πyπx+πy​(ηx+ηy))​.(\eta_{x},\eta_{y})\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\pi_{x}}{\pi_{x}+\pi_{y}}&\frac{\pi_{y}}{\pi_{x}+\pi_{y}}\\[5.69046pt] \frac{\pi_{x}}{\pi_{x}+\pi_{y}}&\frac{\pi_{y}}{\pi_{x}+\pi_{y}}\end{pmatrix}=(\tfrac{\pi_{x}}{\pi_{x}+\pi_{y}}(\eta_{x}+\eta_{y}),\tfrac{\pi_{y}}{\pi_{x}+\pi_{y}}(\eta_{x}+\eta_{y}))\,\text{.}

This recovers the weighted averaging process considered in, e.g., [AL12, QS23]; the corresponding mean-field block dynamics was studied in [CQS24]. The probability measure δπ\delta_{\pi} is invariant and, under the usual connectivity assumption (1.36) on the hypergraph induced by ww, it is the unique invariant probability measure.

In fact, averaging processes satisfy the stronger one-particle spectral gap identity. For pairwise blocks, this was proved in [QS23, Theorem 2.1]; in the present block setting, it also follows by combining (5.26) with Theorem 1.12. Indeed, writing ℒAVG≔ℒΥAVG\mathcal{L}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle AVG}}\coloneqq\mathcal{L}^{\Upsilon^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle AVG}}}, one has

(7.60) gap⁡(ℒAVG)=gap⁡(ℒAVG|𝒫1)​.{\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle AVG}})={\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle AVG}}|_{\mathscr{P}_{1}})\,\text{.}

The preceding example belongs to a broader class. Suppose that Υ\Upsilon is a finite measure on 𝔐\mathfrak{M} and that there exists a strictly positive probability vector π∈Ω\pi\in\Omega such that

(7.61) π​M=π​,for Υ-a.e. M​.\pi M=\pi\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{for $\Upsilon$-a.e.\ $M$}\,\text{.}

Thus, π\pi is invariant for Υ\Upsilon-almost every MM. Consequently, δπ\delta_{\pi} is invariant for the stochastic exchange model, while π⊗k\pi^{\otimes k} is invariant for LkΥL_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} for every k≥1k\geq 1, since π⊗k​M⊗k=π⊗k\pi^{\otimes k}M^{\otimes k}=\pi^{\otimes k} for Υ\Upsilon-almost every MM. If, more strongly,

(7.62) Dπ​M=M𝖳​Dπ​,for Υ-a.e. M​,D_{\pi}M=M^{\mathsf{T}}D_{\pi}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{for $\Upsilon$-a.e.\ $M$}\;\text{,}\;\;

where DπD_{\pi} is the diagonal matrix with diagonal π\pi, then π\pi is reversible for Υ\Upsilon-almost every MM. Indeed, this condition is equivalent to the detailed-balance equation πx​Mx​y=πy​My​x\pi_{x}M_{xy}=\pi_{y}M_{yx}, x,y∈[n]x,y\in[n], and makes M⊗kM^{\otimes k} and LkΥL_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} self-adjoint on L2​(π⊗k)L^{2}(\pi^{\otimes k}). In particular, (7.62) guarantees that spec⁡(ℒΥ|𝒫){\rm spec}(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}|_{\mathscr{P}}) is real.

While (7.61) and (7.62) are equivalent for size-two block updates, for updates involving three or more sites, (7.61) is strictly weaker than (7.62). For example, the cyclic permutation matrix

(7.63) (010001100)\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\\ 1&0&0\end{pmatrix}

preserves the uniform probability vector π≡1/n\pi\equiv 1/n, but is not reversible with respect to it.

Remark 7.8 (Permutations and the interchange process).

Permutation updates provide an interesting degenerate example of stochastic exchange models. Suppose that Υ\Upsilon is supported on n×nn\times n permutation matrices, elements of 𝔐\mathfrak{M}. Starting from a configuration η\eta with pairwise distinct coordinates, and regarding the values (ηx)x∈[n](\eta_{x})_{x\in[n]} as distinct labels, the stochastic exchange model projects onto a block-interchange process; see [CLR10, BC24, AP26].

On the full state space Ω\Omega, however, permutation updates preserve the unordered collection of coordinates of η\eta. Consequently, the dynamics decomposes into infinitely many invariant subsets and admits infinitely many invariant probability measures. In particular, by Proposition 7.6, its spectral gap vanishes. Thus, although Theorem 1.12 applies to permutation updates, the ambient state space Ω\Omega is too large to capture the nontrivial spectral-gap identities of the corresponding interchange-process projections, such as [CLR10, Theorem 1.1] in the graph case and its proposed extensions to hypergraphs [BC24, Conjecture 1.7].

We next give a block version of the immediate exchange model [HP14, Kat15, RS17]. As for the KMP{\rm KMP} model, fix positive parameters α=(αx)x∈[n]\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in[n]} and nonnegative block weights w=(wB)B⊆[n]w=(w_{B})_{B\subseteq[n]}. (7.67) AB=(αx​xαx​yαx​yαy​y)​,αx​x+αx​y=αx​,​αy​y+αy​x=αy​,​αx​y=αy​x​,A^{B}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha_{xx}&\alpha_{xy}\\ \alpha_{xy}&\alpha_{yy}\end{pmatrix}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\alpha_{xx}+\alpha_{xy}=\alpha_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;\alpha_{yy}+\alpha_{yx}=\alpha_{y}\;\text{,}\;\;\alpha_{xy}=\alpha_{yx}\;\text{,}\;\;

and sampling independent random variables U∼Beta⁡(αx​x,αx​y)U\sim{\rm Beta}(\alpha_{xx},\alpha_{xy}), V∼Beta⁡(αy​y,αy​x)V\sim{\rm Beta}(\alpha_{yy},\alpha_{yx}), the update restricted to the coordinates {x,y}\{x,y\} takes the matrix form

The harmonic process [FG22, FFG23] provides an important example for which the update measure is not finite. Fix symmetric conductances bx​y=by​x≥0b_{xy}=b_{yx}\geq 0, with bx​x=0b_{xx}=0, and positive parameters α=(αx)x∈[n]\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in[n]}. (7.75) ex​Hx​y,u=u​ex+(1−u)​ey​.e_{x}H^{xy,u}=ue_{x}+(1-u)e_{y}\,\text{.}

Thus, restricted to the coordinates {x,y}\{x,y\}, the update reads

(7.76) (ηx,ηy)​(u1−u01)=(u​ηx,(1−u)​ηx+ηy)​.(\eta_{x},\eta_{y})\begin{pmatrix}u&1-u\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}=\big(u\eta_{x},(1-u)\eta_{x}+\eta_{y}\big)\,\text{.}

(7.77) ΥHP​(𝑑M)=∑x,y∈[n]bx​y​∫01uαx−11−u​δHx​y,u​(𝑑M)​𝑑u​.\Upsilon^{{\rm\scriptscriptstyle HP}}({\rm d}M)=\sum_{x,y\in[n]}b_{xy}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{u^{\alpha_{x}-1}}{1-u}\,\delta_{H^{xy,u}}({\rm d}M)\,{\rm d}u\,\text{.}

The harmonic process is reversible with respect to μ=Dir⁡(α)\mu={\rm Dir}(\alpha); see [FFG23].

Appendix A Refining Lemma 3.8

This appendix proves the refinement of Lemma 3.8 announced in Remark 3.9, and crucial in the proof of item 2 of Theorems 1.6 and 1.8; see Proposition 5.10. The main result of this section is Proposition A.1. Its proof requires some technical lemmas, inspired by the works [CHM81, BXHR12], and whose complete proofs are postponed to the end of this appendix. The weights α\alpha and ww are fixed throughout, while π=α/α0\pi=\alpha/\alpha_{0} is as in (1.84).

Before stating the result, recall that supp⁡(Υ∞){\rm supp}(\Upsilon_{\infty}) in (3.31) contains only update matrices of the form KBπK_{B}^{\pi}, one for each B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] with wB>0w_{B}>0. For such a block,

(A.1) KBπ=∑x∈Bπxπ⁡(B)​KBex​,with​π​(B)=∑y∈Bπy​.K_{B}^{\pi}=\sum_{x\in B}\frac{\pi_{x}}{\pi(B)}K_{B}^{e_{x}}\;\text{,}\;\;\quad\text{with}\ \pi(B)=\sum_{y\in B}\pi_{y}\,\text{.}

is invariant under every KBπK_{B}^{\pi}. Therefore, 𝒮Υ∞​(θ)=ℝn\mathcal{S}^{{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}_{\infty}}(\theta)=\mathbb{R}^{n} (cf. (3.20)) cannot hold uniformly over all nonconstant θ\theta. The appropriate full-range statement is instead the analogue of (3.19), that is, (A.5) below.

Proposition A.1.

Assume that the hypergraph induced by ww is minimal; see Section 3.2 and Proposition 3.3. Then, for every nonconstant θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

(A.5) 𝒮Υ∞​(θ)+ℝ​𝟏=ℝn​.\mathcal{S}^{{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}_{\infty}}(\theta)+\mathbb{R}\mathbf{1}=\mathbb{R}^{n}\,\text{.}

Moreover, the hidden model introduced in Section 5.2, whose generator ℒ∞\mathscr{L}_{\infty} is given in (5.17), is 𝒞\mathscr{C}-strongly positive on ℛ=ℛ2,∗\mathscr{R}=\mathscr{R}_{2,\ast}: for every t>0t>0,

(A.6) et​ℒ∞​(𝒞∖{0})⊆int⁡(𝒞)​.e^{t\mathscr{L}_{\infty}}\left(\mathscr{C}\setminus\{0\}\right)\subseteq{\rm int}(\mathscr{C})\,\text{.}

Before presenting the proof of Proposition A.1, we introduce some combinatorial tools related to the theory of partitive families and modular decomposition; see [CHM81] and [BXHR12] for a modern account. In fact, Lemma A.3 below, which constitutes a key ingredient in the proof of Proposition A.1, could alternatively be obtained as a direct consequence of the decomposition theorem for partitive families; see, e.g., [BXHR12, Theorem 2]. Nevertheless, we include an elementary direct proof in order to keep the argument self-contained.

For a symmetric matrix Q=(Qx​y)x,y∈[n]Q=(Q_{xy})_{x,y\in[n]}, a set A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n] is called a QQ-module if every index outside AA sees all indices in AA in the same way, namely,

(A.7) z∉A,x,y∈A⟹Qz​x=Qz​y.z\notin A\;\text{,}\;\;x,y\in A\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad Q_{zx}=Q_{zy}.

Then,

(A.8) ℳ⁡(Q)≔{A⊆[n]:A​ is a Q-module}\mathcal{M}(Q)\coloneqq\left\{A\subseteq[n]:A\text{ is a $Q$-module}\right\}

denotes the family of all QQ-modules.

We first record the only closure property of modules that will be used. We say that two sets A,D⊆[n]A,D\subseteq[n] overlap if A∩DA\cap D, A∖DA\setminus D, and D∖AD\setminus A are all nonempty.

Lemma A.2 (Closure of modules).

If A,D∈ℳ⁡(Q)A,D\in\mathcal{M}(Q) overlap, then

(A.9) A∩D​,​A∪D​,​A∖D​,​D∖A​,​A△D∈ℳ⁡(Q)​.A\cap D\;\text{,}\;\;A\cup D\;\text{,}\;\;A\setminus D\;\text{,}\;\;D\setminus A\;\text{,}\;\;A\mathbin{\triangle}D\in\mathcal{M}(Q)\,\text{.}
Proof.

Let A,D∈ℳ⁡(Q)A,D\in\mathcal{M}(Q) overlap. If x,y∈A∩Dx,y\in A\cap D and z∉A∩Dz\notin A\cap D, then z∉Az\notin A or z∉Dz\notin D, and the module property of the corresponding set gives Qz​x=Qz​yQ_{zx}=Q_{zy}. Hence, A∩D∈ℳ⁡(Q)A\cap D\in\mathcal{M}(Q).

Next, let x,y∈A∪Dx,y\in A\cup D and z∉A∪Dz\notin A\cup D. If x,yx,y both belong to AA or both to DD, the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise, after exchanging xx and yy, we may assume that x∈A∖Dx\in A\setminus D and y∈D∖Ay\in D\setminus A. Choosing u∈A∩Du\in A\cap D, we obtain

(A.10) Qz​x=Qz​u=Qz​y​.Q_{zx}=Q_{zu}=Q_{zy}\,\text{.}

Thus, A∪D∈ℳ⁡(Q)A\cup D\in\mathcal{M}(Q).

Consider now A∖DA\setminus D. Let x,y∈A∖Dx,y\in A\setminus D and z∉A∖Dz\notin A\setminus D. If z∉Az\notin A, the module property of AA applies. Otherwise, z∈A∩Dz\in A\cap D. Choose u∈D∖Au\in D\setminus A. Since x,y∉Dx,y\notin D, u∉Au\notin A, and QQ is symmetric,

(A.11) Qz​x=Qx​z=Qx​u=Qu​x=Qu​y=Qy​u=Qy​z=Qz​y​.Q_{zx}=Q_{xz}=Q_{xu}=Q_{ux}=Q_{uy}=Q_{yu}=Q_{yz}=Q_{zy}\,\text{.}

Hence, A∖D∈ℳ⁡(Q)A\setminus D\in\mathcal{M}(Q), and the same argument with AA and DD exchanged gives D∖A∈ℳ⁡(Q)D\setminus A\in\mathcal{M}(Q).

Finally, let x,y∈A△Dx,y\in A\mathbin{\triangle}D and z∉A△Dz\notin A\mathbin{\triangle}D. The conclusion follows from the difference case if x,yx,y belong to the same one of the two sets A∖DA\setminus D and D∖AD\setminus A. Otherwise, assume that x∈A∖Dx\in A\setminus D and y∈D∖Ay\in D\setminus A. If z∉A∪Dz\notin A\cup D, choose u∈A∩Du\in A\cap D and write Qz​x=Qz​u=Qz​yQ_{zx}=Q_{zu}=Q_{zy}. If z∈A∩Dz\in A\cap D, the module properties of DD and AA give

(A.12) Qx​z=Qx​y​,​Qy​z=Qy​x​.Q_{xz}=Q_{xy}\;\text{,}\;\;Q_{yz}=Q_{yx}\,\text{.}

By symmetry, Qz​x=Qz​yQ_{zx}=Q_{zy}. Therefore, A△D∈ℳ⁡(Q)A\mathbin{\triangle}D\in\mathcal{M}(Q). ∎

Lemma A.3 (Triviality of modules).

Let Q=(Qx​y)x,y∈[n]Q=(Q_{xy})_{x,y\in[n]} be symmetric, and suppose that every B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] with wB>0w_{B}>0 is a QQ-module, see (A.7). If the hypergraph induced by ww is minimal, then there exists c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} such that

(A.13) Qx​y=c​,x≠y​.Q_{xy}=c\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad x\neq y\,\text{.}
Proof.

Fix the family ℳ⁡(Q)\mathcal{M}(Q) in (A.8). Call a module A∈ℳ⁡(Q)A\in\mathcal{M}(Q) strong if it overlaps no member of ℳ⁡(Q)\mathcal{M}(Q).

Step 1: the only nonempty proper strong modules are the singletons. Strong modules form a laminar family: two intersecting strong modules are comparable by inclusion. Every singleton is strong and, since [n][n] is finite, is contained in a maximal proper strong module. Let

(A.14) N1,…,NmN_{1},\ldots,N_{m}

be the distinct maximal proper strong modules. They are pairwise disjoint and cover [n][n], and hence

(A.15) [n]=N1⊔⋯⊔Nm​.[n]=N_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup N_{m}\,\text{.}

This partition is compatible with every module in ℳ⁡(Q)\mathcal{M}(Q). Indeed, if A∈ℳ⁡(Q)A\in\mathcal{M}(Q) meets NiN_{i}, then, since NiN_{i} is strong, either A⊆NiA\subseteq N_{i} or Ni⊆AN_{i}\subseteq A. Thus, either AA is contained in one atom of (A.15), or it is the union of all atoms that it meets.

In particular, (A.15) is ww-compatible, because every block BB with wB>0w_{B}>0 belongs to ℳ⁡(Q)\mathcal{M}(Q). Minimality excludes 1<m<n1<m<n, while m≠1m\neq 1 because every NiN_{i} is proper. Therefore, m=nm=n, and every NiN_{i} is a singleton. Since every proper strong module is contained in a maximal proper one, the claim follows.

Step 2: there exists a two-element module. Minimality, together with w[n]=0w_{[n]}=0, ensures that some block BB with wB>0w_{B}>0 satisfies

(A.16) 2≤|B|≤n−1​.2\leq\left\lvert B\right\rvert\leq n-1\,\text{.}

Indeed, if every positive-weight block were a singleton, the two-atom partition [n]={1}⊔([n]∖{1})[n]=\{1\}\sqcup([n]\setminus\{1\}) would be ww-compatible.

Choose A∈ℳ⁡(Q)A\in\mathcal{M}(Q) with 2≤|A|≤n−12\leq\left\lvert A\right\rvert\leq n-1 and minimal cardinality. By Step 1, AA is not strong, so there exists D∈ℳ⁡(Q)D\in\mathcal{M}(Q) overlapping AA. Lemma A.2 gives

(A.17) A∩D∈ℳ⁡(Q)​,​A∖D∈ℳ⁡(Q)​.A\cap D\in\mathcal{M}(Q)\;\text{,}\;\;A\setminus D\in\mathcal{M}(Q)\,\text{.}

Both sets are nonempty proper subsets of AA. By the minimality of |A|\left\lvert A\right\rvert, they are singletons, and hence |A|=2\left\lvert A\right\rvert=2.

Step 3: all two-element sets are modules. Define a relation on [n][n] by

(A.18) x∼y⟺x=yor{x,y}∈ℳ(Q).x\sim y\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad x=y\quad\text{or}\quad\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{M}(Q)\,\text{.}

This is an equivalence relation. Only transitivity requires verification: if x,y,zx,y,z are pairwise distinct and {x,y},{y,z}∈ℳ⁡(Q)\{x,y\},\{y,z\}\in\mathcal{M}(Q), these two modules overlap, and their symmetric difference {x,z}\{x,z\} belongs to ℳ⁡(Q)\mathcal{M}(Q) by Lemma A.2.

Every equivalence class CC belongs to ℳ⁡(Q)\mathcal{M}(Q). Indeed, this is clear for singletons. Otherwise, fix x0∈Cx_{0}\in C and enumerate C={x0,x1,…,xr}C=\{x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\}. Starting from {x0,x1}∈ℳ⁡(Q)\{x_{0},x_{1}\}\in\mathcal{M}(Q), repeatedly apply the union part of Lemma A.2 to the overlapping modules already constructed and {x0,xk}\{x_{0},x_{k}\}, k=2,…,rk=2,\ldots,r.

We claim that every equivalence class CC is strong. Suppose otherwise, and choose D∈ℳ⁡(Q)D\in\mathcal{M}(Q) of minimal cardinality among the modules overlapping CC. Fix

(A.19) x∈D∩C​,​y∈C∖D​,​z∈D∖C​.x\in D\cap C\;\text{,}\;\;y\in C\setminus D\;\text{,}\;\;z\in D\setminus C\,\text{.}

Since x∼yx\sim y, one has {x,y}∈ℳ⁡(Q)\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{M}(Q).

First, D∩C={x}D\cap C=\{x\}. Otherwise, choosing x′∈(D∩C)∖{x}x^{\prime}\in(D\cap C)\setminus\{x\}, the modules DD and {x,y}\{x,y\} overlap. Lemma A.2 then gives

(A.20) D∖{x,y}=D∖{x}∈ℳ⁡(Q)​.D\setminus\{x,y\}=D\setminus\{x\}\in\mathcal{M}(Q)\,\text{.}

This set still overlaps CC: it contains x′∈Cx^{\prime}\in C, misses y∈Cy\in C, and contains z∉Cz\notin C. Its cardinality is smaller than that of DD, a contradiction.

Set O≔D∖{x}=D∖CO\coloneqq D\setminus\{x\}=D\setminus C. Again by Lemma A.2, O∈ℳ⁡(Q)O\in\mathcal{M}(Q). We show that OO is a singleton. Suppose that |O|≥2\left\lvert O\right\rvert\geq 2. Then OO is a nontrivial proper module and, by Step 1, is not strong. Choose H∈ℳ⁡(Q)H\in\mathcal{M}(Q) overlapping OO.

If x∉Hx\notin H, then DD and HH overlap, and Lemma A.2 gives D∖H∈ℳ⁡(Q)D\setminus H\in\mathcal{M}(Q). Since D∩H≠∅D\cap H\neq\varnothing, it is smaller than DD, a contradiction.

If x∈Hx\in H and H⊆DH\subseteq D, then HH itself overlaps CC: it contains x∈Cx\in C and a point of H∩O⊆[n]∖CH\cap O\subseteq[n]\setminus C, while it misses y∈Cy\in C. Moreover, O∖H≠∅O\setminus H\neq\varnothing, so |H|<|D|\left\lvert H\right\rvert<\left\lvert D\right\rvert, again a contradiction.

Finally, if x∈Hx\in H and H⊈DH\not\subseteq D, then DD and HH overlap, and Lemma A.2 gives D∩H∈ℳ⁡(Q)D\cap H\in\mathcal{M}(Q). This set contains x∈Cx\in C and a point of O∩H⊆[n]∖CO\cap H\subseteq[n]\setminus C, while it misses y∈Cy\in C; hence it overlaps CC. Since O∖H≠∅O\setminus H\neq\varnothing, it is smaller than DD, which is impossible.

Consequently, O={z}O=\{z\} for some z∉Cz\notin C. But then D={x,z}∈ℳ⁡(Q)D=\{x,z\}\in\mathcal{M}(Q), so x∼zx\sim z, contradicting x∈Cx\in C and z∉Cz\notin C. Thus, every equivalence class is strong.

By Step 2, at least one equivalence class contains two distinct points. Since this class is strong, Step 1 forces it to be [n][n]. Therefore,

(A.21) {x,y}∈ℳ⁡(Q)​,x≠y​.\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{M}(Q)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad x\neq y\,\text{.}

We may now conclude. Fix x∈[n]x\in[n]. For distinct y,z∈[n]∖{x}y,z\in[n]\setminus\{x\}, the module property of {y,z}\{y,z\} gives

Hence, there exists cx∈ℝc_{x}\in\mathbb{R} such that Qx​y=cxQ_{xy}=c_{x} for every y≠xy\neq x. If x≠yx\neq y, symmetry yields

(A.23) cx=Qx​y=Qy​x=cy​.c_{x}=Q_{xy}=Q_{yx}=c_{y}\,\text{.}

Thus, all the cxc_{x} coincide, proving (A.13). ∎

We are finally in shape to present the proof of Proposition A.1.

Proof of Proposition A.1.

Decompose ℝn=ℋ1,∗⊕ℝ​𝟏\mathbb{R}^{n}=\mathscr{H}_{1,\ast}\oplus\mathbb{R}\mathbf{1}, where ℋ1,∗⊆ℝn\mathscr{H}_{1,\ast}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is given in (A.4). for some c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. Since P​𝟏=𝟏P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}, (A.26) yields

Finally, fix a nonconstant θ∈ℝn\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and let θ¯≔θ−π⁡(θ)​𝟏\bar{\theta}\coloneqq\theta-\pi(\theta)\mathbf{1}. Since θ\theta is nonconstant, 0≠θ¯∈ℋ1,∗0\neq\bar{\theta}\in\mathscr{H}_{1,\ast}. The linear span

Appendix B Feller property of stochastic exchange models

In this section we present the proof Proposition 7.1, which essentially amounts to verify the standard criteria in [Lig05].

Proof of Proposition 7.1.

For every η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega and M∈𝔐M\in\mathfrak{M}, using that the rows of MM are probability vectors,

(B.1) ‖ηM−η‖1≔∑x∈[n]|(ηM)x−ηx|≤∑x∈[n]‖Mx⋅−ex‖1=2∑x∈[n](1−Mx​x).\textstyle\left\lVert\eta M-\eta\right\rVert_{1}\coloneqq\sum_{x\in[n]}|(\eta M)_{x}-\eta_{x}|\leq\sum_{x\in[n]}\left\lVert M_{x{\,\cdot\,}}-e_{x}\right\rVert_{1}=2\sum_{x\in[n]}\left(1-M_{xx}\right)\,\text{.}

Now fix k≥0k\geq 0 and f∈𝒫kf\in\mathscr{P}_{k}. Since ff is Lipschitz on the compact set Ω\Omega, (B.1) and (7.2) show that the integral in (7.6) is well defined. Moreover, for every M∈𝔐M\in\mathfrak{M}, the map η↦f⁡(η​M)−f⁡(η)\eta\mapsto f(\eta M)-f(\eta) belongs to 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k}, with MM-dependent coefficients which, by 0≤Mx​y≤10\leq M_{xy}\leq 1 and the preceding bound, are all Υ\Upsilon-integrable under (7.2). Thus, the integral in (7.6) is well defined and belongs to 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k}, proving the first inclusion in (7.8).

Similarly, for θ∈[a,b]n\theta\in[a,b]^{n},

(B.2) ‖M​θ−θ‖1=∑x∈[n]|∑y≠xMx​y​(θy−θx)|≤(b−a)​∑x∈[n](1−Mx​x)​.\textstyle\left\lVert M\theta-\theta\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{x\in[n]}|\sum_{y\neq x}M_{xy}\left(\theta_{y}-\theta_{x}\right)|\leq(b-a)\sum_{x\in[n]}\left(1-M_{xx}\right)\,\text{.}

Thus, the same argument yields the well definition of ℒΥ\mathscr{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} on ℛ|[a,b]n\mathscr{R}|_{[a,b]^{n}}, and the second inclusion in (7.8).

Given these facts, the construction follows from the standard theory of Markov pregenerators. We treat only ℒΥ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}, the argument for ℒΥ\mathscr{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} being identical.

According to [Lig05, Definition I.2.1], (ℒΥ,𝒫)(\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon},\mathscr{P}) is a Markov pregenerator on 𝒞⁡(Ω)\mathcal{C}(\Omega). Indeed, 𝒫\mathscr{P} given in (7.5) is dense in 𝒞⁡(Ω)\mathcal{C}(\Omega), contains the constants, ℒΥ​𝟏=0\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}\mathbf{1}=0, and ℒΥ\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} satisfies the positive minimum principle: if f∈𝒫f\in\mathscr{P} and η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega satisfy f⁡(η)=minΩ⁡ff(\eta)=\min_{\Omega}f, then

(B.3) ℒΥ​f​(η)=∫Υ⁡(𝑑M)​(f⁡(η​M)−f⁡(η))≥0​,\textstyle\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon}f(\eta)=\int\Upsilon({\rm d}M)\,\left(f(\eta M)-f(\eta)\right)\geq 0\;\text{,}\;\;

since η​M∈Ω\eta M\in\Omega for every M∈𝔐M\in\mathfrak{M}. By [Lig05, Proposition I.2.2], this yields condition (c) in [Lig05, Definition I.2.1]. Moreover, for every λ>0\lambda>0, (I−λ​ℒΥ)​𝒫=𝒫(I-\lambda\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon})\mathscr{P}=\mathscr{P}. Indeed, by (7.8), I−λ​ℒΥI-\lambda\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} leaves each 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} invariant, and it is injective there by the positive minimum principle; hence, by finite dimensionality of the space 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k}, it is bijective.

Therefore, by [Lig05, Propositions I.2.5–6], the closure ¯​ℒΥ\bar{}\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} is a Markov pregenerator and I−λ​¯​ℒΥI-\lambda\bar{}\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} has closed range. Since this range contains the dense subspace 𝒫\mathscr{P}, it equals 𝒞⁡(Ω)\mathcal{C}(\Omega). Thus, ¯​ℒΥ\bar{}\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle\Upsilon} is a Markov generator [Lig05, Definition I.2.7] and, by [Lig05, Theorem I.2.9], generates a unique Feller process on Ω\Omega. ∎

Notation guide

For the reader’s convenience, we collect the main recurring notation in order of appearance. All objects are defined at the indicated locations. Superscripts indicate restrictions to a block, as in αB\alpha^{B} and ηB\eta^{B}, whereas parentheses denote the corresponding total masses, as in α⁡(B)=∑x∈Bαx\alpha(B)=\sum_{x\in B}\alpha_{x} and η⁡(B)=∑x∈Bηx\eta(B)=\sum_{x\in B}\eta_{x}. Conditional quantities are denoted by μB​(f)\mu_{B}(f) and πx|B=πB​(𝟏x)=π⁡(𝟏x∣B)=πx/π⁡(B)\pi_{x|B}=\pi_{B}(\mathbf{1}_{x})=\pi(\mathbf{1}_{x}\mid B)=\pi_{x}/\pi(B). For a linear operator AA defined on a vector space of functions, gap⁡(A){\rm gap}(A) always denotes the smallest (real part of an) eigenvalue of −A-A, possibly excluding the eigenvalue associated to constant functions.
